CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
 
1.1 Head-wise Projections and allocations at BE 2023-24 for Demand No. 51 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.1.1 The Committee finds, from the above -mentioned information, that allocations under several 
heads of Demand No. 51 have been less than the projected figures. Noticeable among them are some 
important heads such as the allocations made for Central Police Reser ve Police Force, Indo-Tibetan 
Border Police, Assam Rifles and Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB), Modernization Plan IV, Delhi Police, 
Police Infrastructure and Border Area Development Programme (BADP). The Committee observes 
that such decrease in allocations are l ikely to affect many important schemes under these heads, and 
may inter-alia, slow down the modernization programmes of Central Armed Police Forces and Delhi 
Police. Similarly lower allocations against the projections of the year 2023- 24 may affect the 
execution of developmental projects particularly in border areas. Hence, the Committee, 
recommends, that the MHA may take up with the Ministry of Finance to increase the allocations 
under these heads in consonance with their projections so that the developmental schemes under 
these heads do not get hampered due to want of sufficient funds.  
 
(Para 2.5.3 of 242nd Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The recommendations of the Committee have been noted.  The matter will be taken up with 
the Ministry of Finance at RE 2023-24 stage if the additional funds will be required. 
1.2 Budgetary Allocation (2023-24) of Demand No. (52-59) for Union Territories 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.2.1 The Committee notes that the fund utilization in the UT of Ladakh is improving. But it is 
still below 50% (as per figures provided by the MHA till 31.01.2023). The Committee appreciates 
the efforts of the Ministry and the UT administration for improvement in fund utilization in Ladakh 
and recommends that the MHA may try to optimize utilization of funds in Ladakh in the next 
financial year. The Ministry of Home Affairs, being the controlling Ministry, may ensure timely 
release of funds to coincide with the working season of the UT of Ladakh. 
 
(Para 2.6.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.2.2 The utilization of funds has improved substantially in the financial year 2022- 23 as 
compared to the financial year 2021- 22. Expenditure of ₹4179.66 crores (70.15%) was incurred in 
the financial year 2022-23 out of the BE of ₹5958 crores as compared to ₹3795.78 crores (63.71%) 
in the  financial year 2021- 22. The recommendation and suggestion of the committee have been 
noted and the capacity of the UT to utilize the funds will be further improved. 
 
1.3 Demand No. 49 on Official Language 
 
 
 
 

 
3 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.3.1 The Committee notes the steps taken by the Department of Official Language (DOL) for the 
promotion of Hindi language in the country. The Committee opines that the documents introduced 
in Parliament like Bills, all Central Acts, Ordinances, Subordinate Legislations etc. as well as the 
judgments of the courts should be translated in Hindi. The Department of Official Language should 
take up with the Legislative Department of the Ministry of Law and Justice for translation of these 
documents. Easy and simple words could be used so that common man can easily understand and 
interpret it. Efforts should also be made for the timely preparation and publication of standard Legal 
Glossary and availability of it in Hindi and other Eighth Schedule Languages as well. The 
Committee hopes that with the enhanced allocation this year under this head, the schemes planned 
by the MHA are implemented and the funds are properly utilized. 
 (Para 3.2.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.3.2 Hindi terms and expressions used in Hindi text of Central Bills, Acts, Ordinances, 
Subordinate Legislations and Legal Glossary etc. prepared by Official Languages Wing.  
Legislative Department were determined and approved by the various experts of the erstwhile 
Official Language (Legislative) Commission.  The C ommission consisted of eminent legal and 
linguistic experts of India and the Hindi text of the most of the important Acts was finalized by them.  
However, an attempt is made to use such terms and expressions by which language can be 
simplified further and the legal language is comprehensible to the general public.  The process of 
law making is a continuous process, wherein attempts are made to incorporate legal and technical 
terms and expressions which the general public can easily understand. 
 
1.3.3 Hindi texts of some important judgments of the Supreme Court and High Courts are being 
published by the Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan of the Legislative Department of the Ministry of Law and 
Justice.  As per the latest information, the issues of UchchtamNyayalaya Nirnay Patrika upto 
February 2022, UchchNyayalaya Civil Nirnay Patrika upto April 2021 and UchchNyayalayaDandik 
Nirnay Patrika, upto July 2021 have been uploaded on the website of the Legislative Department 
and are available for the readers. 
 
1.3.4 Apart from this, Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan, on the request of Hon’ble Supreme Court in 
January 2023 has made available to the Supreme Court the Hindi texts of judgements published in 
the UchchtamNyayalaya Nirnay Patrika from 1968 till date. This includes about ten thousand 
judgements translated into Hindi.  The Supreme Court has uploaded these judgements on their 
ESCR portal http://main.scci.gov.in/e-SCR for public viewing. 
 
1.3.5 Standard Law books including dictionaries are also published by Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan 
of the Legislative Department.  These books are written by eminent authors of law and vetted by 
Editors.  As per the latest information, a total of 34 books have been published by the Vidhi Sahitya 
Prakashan in its authority. 
 
1.4 National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.4.1 The MHA has informed the Committee that the NDRF has been allocated ₹ 1601.02 crores 
against the projected amount of ₹ 1704.98 crores. The Committee notes that aga inst the projected 
demand and the allocation in BE 2023- 24, there is a shortfall to the tune of ₹  100 crores. The 
Committee hopes that this shortfall will not affect the process of raising of new battalions of the 
NDRF. The Committee urges the MHA to take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance and seek 

 
4 
 
this amount at RE stage so that the requirement of additional personnel in NDRF can be fulfilled on 
time to meet the nations demand during exigency. 
 
 (Para 3.3.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.4.2 NDRF has been allocated an amount of Rs.1706.04 crore in Budge t Estimates 2023- 24. In 
case, additional funds are required by NDRF, the same will be projected at RE stage 2023-24. 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.4.3 The Committee notes that 1 lakh volunteers will be trained by NDRF under Aapda Mitra 
Scheme for 350 disaster prone District in the country which will be 285 volunteers per district on an 
average. However, the MHA has not given any timelines by which the Ministry proposes to train 
and raise these volunteers. It also notes that the information regarding the ratio of the volunteers to 
the populations that they are going to cover has also not been provided. The Committee would like 
to be apprised about the details of the plan in this regard. 
(Para 3.3.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.4.4 Aapda Mitra Scheme is being i mplemented by National Disaster Management Authority 
(NDMA) at a total cost of Rs.369.41 Crore in 350 highly vulnerable districts in order to train 
100000 community volunteers by March -2024 which is being funded from Preparedness and 
Capacity Building Funding Window of National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF). All trained 
volunteers will be provided an Emergency Responder Kit (ERK) including an insurance covering 
death/permanent disablement/hospitalization. In all 350 Districts, a list of equipment under 
Emergency Essential Resource Reserve (EERR) will be reserved.  
 
1.4.5     86,113 volunteers have been trained till 30.06.2023. The targets of the scheme will be 
achieved by 31.03.2024. State/UT wise number of volunteers was decided based on the population

increased over the past few years in the changing weather and ecological scenario across the globe. 
The Committee understands the role and responsibilities of NDRF has  also increased manifold in

the time of disasters.

1.6 National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.6.1 With regard to the implementation of works on Early Warning Dissemination System 
(EWDS) and Cyclone Risk Mitigation Infrastructure (CRMI) for Goa and Karnataka, the Committee 
notes that the progress of work in these States are extremely slow. The MHA has also not given 
details regarding the projected tasks to be covered during the dedicated time frames and the 
achievements made by these States. The picture, hence, in this regard is not clear. Nevertheless, the 
Committee recommends that the MHA may take up the matter with the States under Phase II of 
NCRMP and remove the bottlenecks to speed up the creation of i nfrastructures under EWDS and 
CRMI, so that the projects get completed within the stipulated time. The Committee would like to 
be apprised about the status of implementation of the project in Maharashtra and West Bengal. 
  
(Para 3.5.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.6.2 The current status of the physical progress of the works taken up in NCRMP -II in the States 
is enclosed as Annexure - A. It may be seen that 100 % progress has been achieved in most of the 
activities, except mostly for EWDS component. There was slow pr ogress in EWDS due to the 
technical complexities and poor capacity of few contractors. Further, there was delay on account of 
certain permissions needed from Department of Telecommunication. The matter of slow progress 

 
8 
 
had been reviewed extensively with th e States and the design of EWDS was simplified in view of the 
latest advancements which facilitated speedier execution. Even for the remaining incomplete

1.6.3 The EWDS for the States of Maharashtra, West Bengal and Gujarat was not taken up under 
NCRMP II and this is being proposed in the next phase of NCRMP. 
 
1.7 Attrition of CAPF Personnel 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.7.1 The Committee takes note of the suicide and attrition in Central Armed Police Forces 
(CAPFs) during the past 5 years. From the information provided in the table pertaining to the 
‘attrition due to other reasons', the Committee notes that the attrition rates have arisen significantly 
in the case of Assam Rifles and Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), remained similar in case of 
Border Security Force (BSF) and Central Reserve P olice Force (CRPF) and Indo -Tibetan Border 
Police (ITBP) while reduced in case of Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) during 2022, over the previous 
year's figures. The Committee is of the view that such a level of attrition may affect the working 
conditions in the CAPFs. Therefore, urgent measures may be taken to improve the working 
conditions significantly to motivate the personnel to stay in the force. 
 
(Para 4.5.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.7.2 The following steps have been adopted in CAPFs for stress management counselling of 
personnel to improve the working conditions significantly to motivate the personnel: 
 Organizing Chopal system to reduce the stress of Jawans. 
 Strengthening/Revamping of Grievance Redressal system. 
 Regular physical activities, Team Games, Yoga, Cultural programs, Celebration of various 
festivals. 
 Courses on stress management, personality development, psychiatric disorders and topics on 
suicides are being discussed compulsorily. 
 A Grievance Management System has been introduced. A dedicated Mobile/Smart phone with 
internet facility installed in c/room for all personnel to lodge their grievances in the form of 
Voice call/SMS and WhatsApp message which is being effectively monitored by Nodal officers & 
HOO at Unit/office level, Range, Sector Zone &Dte through reports. In this regard, a monthly 
random survey about awareness of this system is being conducted. 
 24x7 toll free number (CRPF -18005990019 of DoEPWD has been circulated at force level so 
that the Force personnel could approach the psychologist for counselling. 
 Providing a respectable infrastructure to CAPFs personnel. 
 Better road connectivity upto the CAPFs posts. 
 Better mobile/internet connectivity has been provided in CRPF camp for utilization of Jawans 
for entertainment as well as for speeding of office work. 
 Facilities of Chopper and Air courier has been provided to CAPFs for utilization of Jawans 
deployed in interior areas. 
 6 Field Hospitals have been raised in Chhattisgarh for providing better medical facilities to 
Jawans. MHA has accorded sanction of Rs.12.06 crore for their up- gradation and developing of 
infrastructure. 
 Field Surgical Units (FSUs) have been raised by conducting training programmes in AIIMS 
Delhi and AIIMS Raipur,  

 
9 
 
 Better equipment for night surveillance has been provided to the CAPFs troops. 
 Camps have been fortified with advanced defence mechanism and system in sensitive areas of 
J&K and LWE areas. 
 Courses on handling of IED have been imparted  
 More Bullet Proof vehicle is being provided to units in J&K and LWE areas. 
 Buddy pair practice is being adopted during operation for 360º security. 
 Every personnel is interviewed by the respective company commanders as well as by the 
Commandant prior to proceeding on leave/temporary duty and post re-joining also. This process 
provides another platform for the personnel to project any issues being faced by them. 
 All Headquarter locations have family accommodations and therefore, individuals have been 
provided with an opportunity to stay with their family for at least 100 days. In unit location at 
field areas, 60 days Earned Leave and 15 days Casual Leave is authorized. In addition, journey 
period (on average 10- 12 days) suffix, inter -fix and prefix is also being availed by the troops. 
There by ensuring 100 days with the families. 
 
1.7.3 Frequent Sainik Sammelans held by commanders at all levels also provide a platform in 
which Jawans are free to present their problems. 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.7.4 The Committee also recommends that the CAPFs may follow a rotation policy of 
deployment so that the jawans do not stay in tough and inhospitable conditions for longer durations 
at a stretch. The Committee is of the view that this could help in reducing not only the tendency to 
seek transfers to preferred locations but also help in addressing attrition to a certain extent. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry should conduct exit interviews or surveys among 
the personnel opting for voluntary retirement and resignation to assess the factors leading to attrition 
and undertake appropriate measures to address the concerns of the personnel so that attrition in the 
Force can be curbed. 
 
(Para 4.5.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.7.5 A rotation policy for transfer of officers/jawans from one place to another already exists in 
CAPFs & AR. The personnel are accordingly rotated after completion of their tenure prescribed in 
the transfer policy from Hard/field areas to soft/static posting. Further, for redressal of posting 
related grievances, an objective and transparent grievance redressal m echanism/software exists in

1.11 Modernization Plan IV of CAPFs 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.11.1 The Committee notes that under Modernization Plan IV of CAPFs, the sanctioned outlay is 
₹1523.16 crores. Out of this, ₹ 248.30 crores was sanctioned for 2022 -23 at BE stage. However, it 
was reduced to ₹ 154.40 crores at RE and the total expenditure that could be made by all the CAPFs 
under this head till 7th February, 2023 has been stated to be ₹  22.16 crores. The Committee  notes 
that of the total sanctioned amount, the expenditure is 14.35%.  
(Para 4.9.5 ibid) 
 
1.11.2 The Committee further notes that against the expenditure of ₹  22.16 crore by the 7 CAPFs, 
Assam Rifles has spent ₹ 14.21 crore, CRPF has spent ₹  3.97 crore, CISF has  spent ₹ 2.74 crore 
while BSF has spent ₹ 1.24 crore. ITBP, NSG and SSB have not started any of their schemes under 
this programme and have reported NIL expenditure. The Committee notes that last year too, some 
CAPFs had reported low e xpenditure under Mode rnization Plan III. The Committee observes that 
persistent low utilization/NIL utilization by the CAPFs under such an important programme is not a 
healthy trend. It wonders that when the CAPFs have themselves been repeatedly requesting for 
upgrading and modernization, what could be the reasons for the low utilization of funds. The 
Committee feels that it will also lead to a delay in the procurement of weapons and other 
technological equipments, which in turn will affect the capabilities  of CAPFs. Hence, the 
Committee recommends that the MHA direct the CAPFs to remove the bottlenecks hampering the 
modernization plans of CAPFs and set up a monitoring mechanism to ensure optimal utilization of 
funds during the next financial year. 
 
(Para 4.9.6 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.11.3 The main reason for underutilization of allocated funds under this Scheme are as under: 
 
 Previous financial year (i.e. 2022- 23) was the first year of implementation of Modernization 
Plan IV. After issuing Scheme guidelines on 25/05/2022, CAPFs could get only eight months 
during financial year 2022-23. 
 Most of the items under this Scheme are highly technical in nature. They are not available in 
domestic market off the shelf. Hence, delivery period of these items are longer res ulting in long 
gestation period and delayed procurement process. 

 
13 
 
 Advance sample(s) provided by participating bidders did not meet the approved Qualitative 
Requirements (QRs), resulting in scrapping of tenders. In some cases, firms were unable to give 
advance sample during the technical evaluation process. 
 Non-availability of QRs/upgraded QRs is a major road block in procurement process under 
Modernization Plan-IV. Due to frequent change in technology, even QRs of so many items that 
are available need revision/upgradation. 
 Successful bidders were unable to supply the ordered items within the agreed delivery period. 
 
1.11.4 This Ministry is closely monitoring the implementation of this Scheme. To ensure optimum 
fund utilization during current financial year, CAPFs have been advised: 
 To set up a dedicated QRs/TDs Cell to expedite the finalization/revision of QRs/TDs for 
approved items under Modernization Plan- IV.  CAPFs have been directed to finalize QRs/TDs 
of approved items by the first quarter of the current FY i.e. 2023-24. 
 CAPFs have been allowed to initiate procurement process for all approved items under 
Modernization Plan-IV, irrespective of funds availability at that particular point of time subject 
to the condition that tendered amount must not exceed 2.5 times of allocated funds for that 
financial year and that the supply order will be placed by the CAPFs concerned only after 
ensuring availability of funds. CAPFs have been sensitized to initiate procurement process for 
items for the current  financial year i.e. (2023-24). 
 Further, a Committee headed by AS (CIS&PM) with JS(JKL), JS(BM -I) and representative of  
LWE Division, MHA, O/o Principal Scientific Adviser to Govt. of India, DRDO, BPR&D and 
CAPFs as Members has been constituted to critically analyze the needs of  CAPFs including 
Action Plan, Procurement Plan for 5 years, Modernization Plan, Gap between authorization and 
holding in CAPFs etc. 
 Lead Force concept for procurement of common weapons, equipment etc. is being followed to 
the extent possible to avoid repetitive efforts for the common items by different CAPFs, has also 
been enforced.

Observation/Recommendation 
 
2.6.1 The Committee notes that there is a vacancy of 25.42% in the Paramedical staff of CAPFs

taken to fill all the vacancies of Para -medical staff of the CAPFs in a time -bound manner. The 
Committee further recommends that the CAPFs may explore the feasibility of recruitment on an ad -
hoc basis till regular appointments are made for Paramedical staff. The Committee would like to be

2.6.2 The filling up of the vacant posts of Paramedical staff authorized in direct recruitment quota 
is under process. The vacancy to be filled up through promotion is already under process which is 
likely to be completed soon. As of now, there is no provision f or recruitment of Paramedical staff on 
ad-hoc basis in Forces. Medical Officers, including specialists, though are being filled on 
contractual basis. 
 
2.6.3 The role of Medical and Paramedical Staff are as follows: 
 

 
27 
 
 Medical & Para-medical Staff in CAPFs pr ovide primary medical cover to the troops and their 
families. The hospitals in which they serve range from the Mini MI rooms in Border 
Outposts/FDLs to 10/20 bedded Hospitals in Battalion and also the 50/100/200 beds in CH/RH. 
 CAPFs Medical Officers provid e primary Medical care at Unit level to the troops and their 
dependents. In composite Hospitals, Specialists Medical Officers provide secondary medical 
cover. Apart from providing medical care, all the Medical Officers including Specialist Medical 
Officers take part in various recruitment procedures conducted throughout the year in various 
types of Medical Boards (Annual Medical Examinations, Review Medical examination etc) 
which are constituted for this purpose. They also provide medical cover during Elect ion Duties, 
Internal Security Duties, Disaster Management or any other duty assigned, as and when 
required. CAPFs Medical Officers are also deployed in areas like High Altitude Areas, Border 
Out Posts in desert areas or in other areas having adverse climat ic condition, where usually the 
Civilian Doctors do not want to perform their duties. They are also entrusted in providing 
Medicare to the AB-PMJAY patients reporting to them. 
 Paramedical staff is an integral part for giving medical support either at far f lung Border Out 
Posts of in any adverse climate as well as at LWE areas also. These Paramedical staff, 
especially the trained Nursing Assistant and Medics, are the backbone or the First Line Medical 
Care providers to the troops where Medical Officers are not immediately available, and during 
patient evacuation. Similarly, Lab. Assistants, Radiographers, Pharmacists, Nurses 
(Male/Female) are the integral part of any Composite Hospital. Trained Nursing Assistants and 
Pharmacists are the important supporting s taff in Unit Hospitals in CAPFs organizations. A 
Medical Set-up without these Paramedical Staff remains incomplete and Medical Officers and 
Paramedical Staff work hand- in-hand to render optimal medical care to the serving personnel 
and their dependents. 
 The available strength of MO/Paramedical Staff of CAPFs is not adequate to provide Medicare 
to the troops and dependents. 
 The following recommendations are proposed in the aforesaid matter: 
 To augment the strength of Paramedical Staff in all existing Hospitals. 
 To explore the feasibilities for appointment of Paramedical staff on contractual /ad- hoc/ 
outsourcing basis to reduce the deficiencies and help in better Medicare to the troops.

2.16 Modernization of Prisons 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
2.16.1 The Committee notes that in some cases, the prison staff including medical personnel of the 
prison hospitals have been found involved in arranging mobile phones and other contraband items 
for the prison inmates. This is due to the fact that the prison staf f stay posted in one prison for long 
period of time. It leads to collusion between them and the prisoners. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the MHA may advise all the States to follow rotational policy for transfers and 
postings of prison staff including medical staff and set a maximum tenure for which a staff can work 
in one prison. The MHA may consider creation of a cadre of prison staff for the Union Territories so 
that the personnel are transferred to different UTs and will not stay posted in one prison of any UT 
for long period of time. This along with the technological interventions for the security of jail cited 
in the Para above, will help in curbing the use of mobile phones and other contraband items by the 
criminals inside prisons. 
 (Para 4.22.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.16.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs, vide letter No. V -17013/11/2022-PR dated 2.5.2022, had 
already advised the States that to discourage complacency and corrupt practices in Prisons, Prison 
staff may be rotated on a regular basi s. They have been advised that the prison staff should be 
transferred to other jails on periodic basis. On the point of creation of a separate cadre of prison 
staff for the Union Territories, it is informed that the Ministry of Home Affairs had assigned th e 
responsibility of examining the feasibility of transfer of prison staff between the Union Territories 
(UTs) to the Bureau of Police Research & Development (BPR&D), who, after receiving responses 
from all UTs, had informed that there are various administr ative and procedural limitations 
regarding transfer of prison staff between UTs, such as difference in Pay Scales, Service Conditions, 
Allowances, Language barriers, etc. Also, NCT of Delhi and Puducherry are UTs with legislature 
and are guided by their own rules and regulations and therefore transfer of Prison Staff between 
UTs was not found practical and viable. 
 
2.16.3 The other recommendations of the Committee are noted and continuous efforts will be made 
to streamline the procedure.

CHAPTER I 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
1.1 Utilization of Funds 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1.1 The Committee notes that, in accordance with the Department of Economic Affairs' 
directives, a revamped mechanism for transferring funds under Central Sector Schemes has been 
implemented. The Committee also notes that the Ministry has been able to utilize around 16% of 
the allocated amount in the first three quarters of the financial year. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may strengthen its coordination mechanism with the NEC, States 
and implementing agencies so that such a situation that arose in the Financial Year 2022 -23 can 
be addressed promptly and without delay in order to maximize the utilization of f unds. The 
Committee also recommends that the Ministry make all-out efforts to ensure that the balance of ₹ 
500 crores is accounted for by the close of the financial year 2022-23. 
(Para 2.3.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
1.1.3 Further, due to the CNA system being brought into effect, in this transition period 2022-  
23, there were two sources of funds for the Schemes of Ministry for the States – from the unspent 
balances of releases made previously; and from the budgetary outlays in RE 2022- 23. In 
addition to the ₹ 2,180 crore spent by the States out of the available balances from the previously 
released advances till FY 2021- 22; further expenditure/ utilization of about ₹ 1,295 crore was 
incurred from available unspent balances including from RE 2022- 23 by the SGs / IAs with 
pursuance from the Ministry of DoNER. 
 
1.1.4 Thus, the total expenditure / utilization in FY 2022-23 by the SGs / IAs in the NE Region 
amounted to nearly ₹ 3,475 crore. 
1.2 Capital Section 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.1 The Committee notes that due to a change in the classification of Head of Account under 
NESIDS, the major part of the budget outlay has been reflected under Capital Section. Hence, 
the total Revenue outlay has decreased to ₹ 1798.75 crores in BE 2023-24 from ₹ 2140.04 crores in 
BE 2022- 23. The Committee also notes that under the head ‘Schemes of NEC’, there is a 
shortfall of ₹ 381.58 crores in BE 2023- 24 compared to the projected demand of ₹ 1181.58 
crores. The Ministry has also informed the Committee that allocated funds may not be adequate. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry coordinate with NEC to prioritize the 
expenditure out of the present budgetary allocation and seek more funds at the RE 2023- 24 stage 
to meet the shortfalls. The Committee also recommends that the requirement of additional funds 
under the Capital Section may also be realistically assessed at the RE stage and additional funds, 
if required, may be sought. 

3  
(Para 2.5.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.2.2 The observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
1.2.3 Moreover, of the total expenditure of nearly ₹ 3,475 crore during 2022- 23, the capital 
expenditure accounted for 94% or about ₹ 3,260 crore – [inclusive of ₹ 600 crore from heads 
under Capital Section; and ₹ 2,660 crore for creation of capital assets from heads under Revenue 
Section]. 
 
1.2.4 For the year 2023- 24, it has been envisaged that out of the planned total expenditure of 
nearly ₹ 5,892 crore, the capital expenditure will account for 92% or ₹ 5,417.28 crore – [ 
inclusive of ₹ 4093.25 crore from heads under Capital Section; and over ₹ 1,324.03 crore for 
creation of capital assets from heads under Revenue Section]. 
 
1.2.5 However, the allocation for the overall holistic development, social infrastructure and 
social development targeted Schemes of NEC is ₹ 800 crore in 2023-24; (~20% higher than) ₹ 
666.87 crore, of the RE 2022-23. 
1.3 Schemes of North East Council 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3.1 The Committee notes the role of the NEC in formulating regional plans for integrated and 
balanced socio-economic development of the NER. The Committee also takes note of the reply 
of NEC that the unspent balance of NEC  schemes has been minimized and that much progress is 
being made. For this, NEC should minimize the queries and consider deputing their officers to 
resolve the issues involved through direct meetings with the State Government officials so that 
the implemen tation process is expedited. The Ministry, being the nodal agency for matters 
relating to the planning, execution and monitoring of development schemes and projects in the 
North Eastern Region, should closely coordinate with NEC to ensure the timely implem entation 
of the projects. 
(Para 3.1.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.3.2 The observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
 
1.4 Capital Section 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.4.1 With regard to the reduced allocation made for the Schemes of NEC, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may coordinate with NEC to prioritize the expenditure out of the 
present budgetary allocation and seek more funds at the RE 2023-24 stage to meet the shortfalls. 
(Para 3.1.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 

4  
1.4.2 The allocation under ‘Schemes of NEC’ at BE 2023- 24 is ₹ 800.00 crore against 
projected demand of ₹ 1181.58 crore. All efforts are being made to fully utilize the budgeted 
outlay. The shortfall of ₹ 381.58 Crore shall be taken up at RE 2023- 24 stage based on actual 
demand prevailing at that point of time. 
 
1.5 Central Pool of Resources for North East and Sikkim /North East Special 
Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.5.1 The Committee notes that in the fiscal year 2022 -23, the Ministry has spent only ₹0.17 
crores against a budget of ₹ 650 crores under the North East Special Infrastructure Development 
Scheme (NESIDS). The reason given for low fund utilization is the introduction of a new process 
for implementing the revised procedure of fund flow under Central Sector Schemes, as has 
already been discussed in the previous chapter. The Ministry has stated that it expects to spend 
₹1104.27 crores by the end of the Financial Year 2022- 23 for the schemes under North East 
Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS), Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources 
(NLCPR) and Hill Area Development Programme (HADP). The Committee observes that there 
is low utilization of funds in the first three quarters of the financial year 2022- 23. Non-utilization 
of funds may put additional pressure on the budget for the Financial Year 2023- 24. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must take appropriate steps to ensure that 
its schemes are carried out on time in the forthcoming Financial Year. 
(Para 3.2.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.5.2 The observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
1.5.3 The need to ramp -up States’ implementing capacities t o measure up to the even higher 
budgetary resources mobilized for the MDoNER schemes for FY 2023 -24 onwards and any 
unspent balances upto end of FY 2022- 23 is being focused and impressed upon the IAs and the 
State Governments of the NE Region and being pursued along with right upto the highest levels. 
 
1.6 North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited 
(NEHHDC) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.6.1 The Committee notes that the North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development

been put in place to monitor the pace and pattern of fund utilization of various projects to 
prevent cost and time overruns. Specifically, Secretary, North Eastern Council (NEC) is a 
member of the PM -DevINE Empowered Inter -Ministerial Committee (EIMC) tasked with the 
following: 
• To recommend effect ive means for Monitoring and Evaluation through field inspection 
inter alia through suitable third-party agencies; 
• To review the progress of project implementation under PM-DevINE. 
 
3.1.3 In addition, the PM -DevINE scheme guidelines, also state that to limit construction risk 
(time and cost over runs), infrastructure projects should be awarded in Engineering-  
Procurement-Construction (EPC) mode, on fixed cost basis, with provision for liquidated 
damages. The tender notices and contracts may also include binding c lauses for incentives to 
contractors for early completion and penal provision for delay. In case of projects worth more 
than ₹100 crore, there should be adequate contractual provisions for concurrent monitoring of 
the projects by an independent third-party agency. All these provisions would limit cost and time 
overruns in PMDevINE projects. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.1.4 The Committee notes the Ministry’s efforts in putting a mechanism in place to limit 
the construction risks of time and cost overruns  for the newly introduced PM -DevINE 
scheme. However, the Committee would also like to bring to the Ministry’s notice that, 
time and again, the implementation and completion of the infrastructural projects under 

18 
various developmental schemes have been affected by the slow pace of projects due to 
varied issues despite many such monitoring mechanism in place. The Committee would like 
to be apprised of the progress made so far for implementation of this scheme. 
3.2 North East Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.1 The Committee notes that, in BE 2023-24, an allocation of ₹ 7.67crores has been made for 
North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) out of which ₹2 crores 
is for capital head and ₹5.67 crores is for revenue head. The Committee is of the considered view 
that various infrastructure facilities related to agriculture and allied services need to be scaled up. 
This will promote Agri-Horti products, allowing them to reach their full potential. Focus needs to 
be given to augment support facilities like transport, storage, sale and profit generation even 
through the remote areas of the NER. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Government consider improving infrastructure support for agriculture and related sectors. 
(Para 3.8.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
3.2.2 NERAMAC has undertaken numerous activities to improve infrastructure support for 
agriculture and other related sectors. NERAMAC’s processing plants of cashew and pineapple 
in Tripura and Ginger in Meghalaya are in various stages of being made operational and are 
expected to be fully functional by mid-2023. Moreover, numerous primary/ secondary processing 
plants for value addition of NER Agri -Horti commodities are planned for FPOs in FY 2023- 24. 
Five Cold storage facilities are being set up in BTC, Assam at the request of the Council. 
NERAMAC is also initiating the process to enroll some FPCs to avail the Agricultural 
Infrastructure Fund supported and promoted by the Ministry of Agriculture  and Farmers 
Welfare. 
F
urther Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.3 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and appreciates the numerous 
activities taken to improve the infrastructure support for agriculture and allied sector. The 
Committee would like to be apprised of all the details pertaining to infrastructure activities 
being undertaken by NERAMAC in NER Region. 
3.3 Civil Aviation
Recommendation/Observation 
3.3.1 The Committee notes the efforts of the Ministry of DoNER and the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation in constructing and operationalizing a number of new airports in NER. North Eastern 
Region connectivity is a critical attribute for the region's overall development. The Committee 
also suggests that a similar impetus may be given and efforts made to operationalize th e 
remaining airports. This will help to promote tourism and last-mile connectivity in NER. The 

19  
Committee would like to be updated on the status of the UDAN scheme's implementation in 
NER, as well as the frequency of flight operations and aircraft types used at these newly 
identified/operational airports 
(Para 4.8.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
3.3.2 The observations/recommendations of the Committee are noted. 
 
3.3.3 Updated status of UDAN Scheme as informed by Ministry of Civil Aviation (MOCA) is 
attached at Annexure-V 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.3.4 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee is of the view that 
air connectivity in the NER is crucial for overall development and last mile reach in the 
region and UDAN scheme can play a huge  role in bolstering the connectivity in the region. 
The Committee desires that the Ministry of DoNER should coordinate with the Ministry of

on the project upto 31.03.2023. An outlay of `1,100 crore has been provided for 2023- 24. The
section from Dhansiri -Sukhovi(16.5 km) has been commissionedand work has been taken up in
remaining length. TDC: March 2026.

connecting Gangtok with IR network (Rangpo is 40 km short of Gangtok). Cost of the project is
`8,043 crore and expenditure of `4865.71 crore has been incurred on the project upto 31.03.2023.
An outlay of `2,250 crore has been provided for 2023- 24. Work on this project has been taken up.
TDC: December 2024. Further, Final Location Survey from Rangpo to Gangtok (40 km) has been
sanctioned in February 2022.
(5) Meghalaya: Two new line projects have been taken up simultaneously for connecting
Shillong, the capital of Meghalaya, with IR network:

crore and expenditure of `1070.77 crore has been incurred on the project upto 31.03.2023. An
outlay of `65 crore has been provided for 2023 -24. 10 km length of the project falling in

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home 
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby 
present this Two Hundred Fifty First Report on Action Taken by Government on the 
Recommendations/Observations Contained in the Two Hundred Forty Fifth  Report of the 
Committee on  ‘Prison – Conditions, Infrastructure, And Reforms’. 
2.  The Two Hundred Forty Fifth  Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of the Lok 
Sabha on the 21 st September, 2023. After presentation/laying of the Report, the copies thereof 
were sent to the Ministry of Home Affairs  requesting them to furnish Action Taken Notes on the 
recommendations of the Committee contained in the Report. The Ministry furnished the Action 
Taken Notes on the said Report to the Committee on 30th January, 2024 and additional 
information on 15th July, 2024.  
3. The Committee has noted that the statement on the status of implementation of the 
recommendations contained in the said Report of the Committee has not been laid on the Table 
of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha by the Ministry.

1.1 Women prisoners 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.1.1 The committee recommends that the babies born in the prison to be allowed to stay with 
mothers until the age of 12 in order to provide a nurturing environment for the children during 
their early years while ensuring their well -being and development. Further, as per guidelines 
issued from time -to-time emphasis should be given towards proper care of children relating to 
food, shelter, medical care, education, and physical growth. Apart from this, sports and 
entertainment facilities are also to be provided to these children.  
 (Para 2.4.7 of 245th Report) 
Action Taken  
1.1.2 ‘Prisons’/‘persons detained therein’ is a “State List” subject under Entry 4 of List II of 
the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. Administration of prisons and prisoners is the 
responsibility of respective State Governments. 
1.1.3 The Report of the Committee has been shared with all States/UTs and they have been 
requested to take appropriate steps to comply with the recommendations made in the Report.  
1.1.4 The Ministry of Home Affairs has also issued an advisory to al l States and Union 
Territories forwarding the guidelines for the welfare of the children of women inmates. These 
guidelines, inter-alia, provide that the children of prison inmates should be provided access to 
education, recreational facilities, food, shel ter and medical assistance etc. The Model Prison 
Manual 2016 circulated by the Ministry of Home Affairs to all States and Union Territories also 
has a specific chapter on “Women Prisoners‟, which, inter -alia, provides that prison 
administration should ensure holistic development of the children of women inmates. The 
Ministry of Home Affairs had also circulated a report to the States/ Union Territories titled 
“Women in Prisons” prepared by the Ministry of Women and Child Development. The report, 
inter-alia, contains specific recommendations on “children of women prisoners” and “better 
living arrangements” for women inmates and their children, etc. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.1.5 The Committee recommends that keeping in mind, the safety, hygiene, and health of 
women, adequate arrangements for separate toilets and bathrooms with proper water supply and 
more specialist women doctors are to be provided in women jails. The Committee al so notes that 
Ministry of Home Affairs should from time to time, instruct all the State Governments/UTs that 
necessary skill development programmes to be provided to the women prisoners which indeed 

3 
 
will help them to find employment after being released fr om the prison. It is also recommended 
that a study may be conducted on women inmates who have been released from jails to evaluate 
the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs, identify areas of concern and to enhance prison 
rehabilitation policy. 
 (Para 2.4.8  ibid) 
Action Taken  
1.1.6 The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has requested the Bureau of Police Research & 
Development (BPR&D) to undertake a study on women inmates who have been released from 
jails to evaluate the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs and provide its recommendation to

programmes designed for women inmates which are as follows: 
a. Economic Model 1: Vocational training programmes and educational  
programmes are conducted to empower the women inmates which will help  
them in starting their own activities 
b. Economic Model 2: Vocational training is provided to women inmates with the  
help of verified & reputed NGOs which in turn employ the women inmates after  
their release 
c. Economic Model 3: Discharged Prisoners Aid Societies (Non- govt. Company)  
have been established in some States which give financial loan to released  
prisoners for their employment 
d. Economic Model 4: Women inmates are given training and are off ered 
employment opportunities at the petrol pumps owned by the Prison 
Departments of the States

them for future employment once they are released from prison. It has been  
concluded in the report that the rehabilitation programmes for women inmates are still

1.2 Prison staff 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.1  The Committee has noted that across all categories of jail staff like -  jail cadre staff, 
warders, correctional staff and medical officers etc., the percentage of vacancies are very, high. It 
has become the most neglected part of the prison administration and it makes the management of 
the prisons very difficult. Having limited staff and making ad hoc arrangements to address staff 
shortage will compromise the security. A critical role is played by the Resident Medical Officers, 
Correctional Staff and Warders in the upkeep of the health conditions of the inmates, reformation 
and rehabilitation of the inmates and safety and security of the prison and prisoners. The 
Committee recommends that all posts need to be filled up immediately and no post should 
remain vacant for more than 3 months. 
 (Para  2.7.3  ibid)

1.11 Library and recreation 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 1.11.1   The Committee is of the view that setting up of libraries in prison can play an important 
role in the rehabilitation of inmates. Library is a storehouse of vast knowledge and information 
which can provide unlimited opportunities to prisoners not only to ga in and upgrade their 
educational skills but also to provide free access to relevant resources which may be crucial for 
their personal growth and overall wellbeing.   It can be a source of alternate and constructive 
recreational activity for prisoners who are fond of reading. The Committee feels that with limited 
fund resources, setting up a library may be a daunting task for prison administration. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the prison administrations which do not have library 

13 
 
facilities in th eir jails, can start by setting up of small library by receiving second -hand books. 
Gradually, a small allocation of funds for upgrading their libraries may be made on regular basis 
to have a well stalked library. The Committee also feels the efforts taken  by States like Tamil 
Nadu, Kerala, Rajasthan, etc. for library facilities in their prisons needs to be appreciated and 
other States have to follow those practices. At the same time, the Ministry may also highlight the 
importance and utility of library facilities by giving advisory to State/UT prison administration in 
this regard. 
 
(Para 4.5.4 ibid) 
Action Taken

1.14  Measures to control criminal activities in prisons 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.14.1   During its interactive sessions with various State/UT Governments, the 
Committee was informed that ganja and cell phones are the common contraband items 
that are most frequently smuggled into the prisons among others. The Tamil Nadu State 
Government inform ed that throw method using catapult is one of the common 
approaches employed to smuggle the contrabands into the prisons. The Committee 
observes that the articles like cell phones inside the prison are used by the inmates to 
operate criminal activities outside the prison. Possession of cell phones in the hands of 
the prisoners can also stir up gang wars inside jails. Usage of ganja and other narcotics 
in prison compromises the reformation and rehabilitation of the inmates. The 
Committee also observes that e -Mulakat, video conferencing etc., will also help reduce 
the smuggling of the contraband into the prison as prisoners can communicate with 
their families through such facilities. The Committee has also noted that the prison 
staffs are helping the prisoners  to get the contraband inside the prison. Keeping in view 
of the negative impact the contrabands can have on reformation of prisoners, the 
Committee recommends that the frisking standards should be enhanced in all the State 
prisons. MHA should set benchmar k frisking standards to curb the entry of contraband 
articles and in turn prevent gang wars. All the State/UT Governments shall comply with 
such standards. Further, drones should be used in prisons to keep an aerial surveillance 
of the prison premises. Sni ffer Dog Squads may also be used in detecting contrabands.  
 (Para 4.10.5 ibid )

Recommendation/Observation 
4.2.1 The Committee has noted that the picture of young offenders is not clear across States. In 
view of this, the Committee recommends that a clear definition of ‘young offenders’ should be 
given by MHA along with a common guideline to all State/UT Governments describing the 
procedure to govern them shall be provided for the convenience of the State/UT Governments. 
State Governments may take steps for holistic development of these young offenders by 
providing all of them with education, skill/vocational training, nutrition. Also, the rate of 
recidivism among this category of inmates may be monitored regularly and a study may be 
conducted to understand the social background of such young offenders.  
 (Para 2.5.3  ibid)

to all States and UTs defines a “Young Offender” as any prisoner who has attained the age of 18

Offenders” and provides guidance to States and UTs for treatment of ‘Young Offenders’. MHA 
regularly follows up the matter regarding adoption of the Model Prison Manual with all States 
and UTs so that the States and UTs can benefit from the guidance provided in the manual.

penalties/disciplinary measures should be set in their conditions of service.

A study report on Effectiveness of Rehabilitation Programmes for Women 
Inmates who have been released from Jail and identify the areas of concern. 
In compliance of MHA OM No.V-17013/55/2023 -PR, dated 11.12.2023 
regarding Effectiveness  of Rehabilitation Programmes  for Women Inmates who 
have been released from Jail and identify area of concern BPR&D has formed a 
study group comprising pr ison officers from Telangana,  Andhra Pradesh, 
Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Delhi. 
The following outcome are emanated from the discussions among the study 
group: - 
Types of economic models of rehabilitation programmes 
Designed for Women Inmates 
Economic model-I 
In this model Vocational Training Programme and Educational Programme are 
conducted to empower women inmates so that ones they are release, they can start 
their own activities while staying with the families. 
• All Prisons conduct vocational Training Programmes in Tailoring
&Stitching, bakery products, Stitching of Jute Bags, Envelope making,
Agarbatti making, Fast food making ,Beautician skills, Flower an d

48 
garlands making, block painting, boutique, artificial jewellery, Sanitary 
Pads and Napkins, Namkeen and Pickle Making, Mehandi, Handicraft 
Classes, Computer Training, Organic Farming, Sports, Yoga and Library 
management, Creche maintenance etc. These courses empower all women 
inmates to make livelihood after release from prisons. 
• Compulsory Adult Education Programme, Padho Padhao Classes for basic
education and spoken English courses are conducted for women inmates to
empower them.
Economic Model-II 
In this model Prison Administration imparts Vocational Training to women 
inmates with the help of verified, reputed NGOs. These NGOs in turn employ the 
women inmates once they are released from the Prisons. 
In some States Prison Administration has collaborated with State 
Government Skill Development Institute that off er recognised 
certificatethatpavethewayforeffectiveemploymentafterreleasefromthePrison. 
Economic Model-III 
Discharged Prisoners Aid Societies(Non- govt company) are established in 
some States which give financial loan to release Prisoners for their employme nt. 
Eg.-TamilNadu. 
Economic Model-IV 
The Prison Administration has its own petrol pumps throughout the State. 
The women inmates are given training and assigned duties while there in the 
Prison and whoever wants employment after their release from the Prison, are 
offered employment opportunities at the petrol pump owned by the Prison 
Department. 
Economic Model-V 
In this model State Government has special schemes for the rehabilitation 
and employment of the released Prisoners 

46 
Financial Assistance to Ex- Convicts” was launched by the Department of 
Social Justice, Government of Kerala. This scheme is implemented by the 
Department of Social Justice to help those released from jail from poor economic 
conditions to find their livelihood. As part of this scheme, one-time financial 
assistance is provided to those released from jail to find self-employment and start 
some small Industry/Trade as part of social rehabilitation. 
In addition to above economic models the following relevant points are also 
observe during the study. 
After care officer: - An officer of the rank of jailor or Dy. Jailor is 
designated for the looking after the needs of released women inmates and helping 
them in shelter homes and admission in school for their children. 
Open Prisons for women inmates (Maharashtra, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh) 
gives an opportunity to women inmates to employ themselves in gainful activities 
and prepare them for future employment once they are released from the Prison. 
Conclusion: - 
The above study reveals that the rehabilitations programmes for release 
women inmates are still in transit phase. There is no uniform structure and policy 
throughout the country in this regard. 
Some NGOs are doing commendable job to rehabilitate released women 
prisoners and it is also observed that State Government sponsored programmes 
benefit the rehabilitations of released women prisoners. 
This is to inform that BPR&D is conducting a study on Stigmatization and 
Victimization of Released Women Prisoners and the ir Children in India, in 
associations with Academy of Prisons and Correctional Administration, Vellore, 
Tamil Nadu. One of the objectives of above study is “ To study the measures, 
schemes available for rehabilitation, reintegration of women prisoners and 
their children in India.” The outcome of the above study will be shared once the 
research is completed.

Report on Parameterising of Training Programmes conducted by 
State Prison Departments and their performance evaluation 
T
o train the Prison Personnel and enabling them to have a dignified approach 
towards the inmates and to bring about the reforms in inmates, the following 
parameters have been laid down for the training programmes: - 
• Human Rights in Prison Administration : Prison Officers shall ensure that
while administering prison, human rights of prisoners are protected. On the
other hand, human rights of prison administration officers and staff are also
of immense importance. Prison personnel should understand the ways and
means of ensuring human rights protection through prison administration.
The rights of Prisoners shall be ensured according to international covenants.
International Legal instruments as well as judicial precedents of India
through which various rights of prisoners are conferred and ensured.
• N
eeds of Vulnerable Groups : The prison officers shall ensure the needs of
vulnerable groups. Prison officers shall be trained in identification of
vulnerable groups of prisoners and their specific issues and work towards
reducing the existing vulnerabilities by adopting and implementing positive
policy level measures.

48 
• Skill Development/Educational Programmes: Skill development of prison
inm
ates is a crucial activity that weans inmates away from  recidivism.
Theses programme is to explore and understand practical ways in which skill
development and educational courses could be undertaken in prisons.
• Rehabilitation and Correctional Programmes : Prison officers shall be
aware of knowledge and skills related to implementation of rehabilitati on
a
nd correctional programmes for the prisoners.
• S
tress Management: Prison Officers shall have necessary knowledge about
stress, sources, effects, management techniques, etc.,
• S
earch Procedures : Invasive body searches lie at the crosshairs of the
fundamental principle inherent under the human rights framework that the
treatment of prisoners should be humane and respect the inherent rights and
dignity of the person.
• L
eadership in Prison Administration : A variety of leadership
competencies are required in order to develop effective leadership in prisons.
A Prison Leader must be able to lead a team and motivate staff to work for
organizational goals and bring reforms and improvements in the prison
system.
• M
anaging Prison Industries: There have been several developments in the
establishment of new industries and the modernization of existing sectors in
response to market trends. Hence Prison Officers need to be trained on this
subject of managing prison industries develop modern Prison Industries or
m
odernize the existing ones.
• G
ender Sensitization : Gender sensitive prison management policies and
practices should be responsive to the needs of women in a holistic manner.
Gender biases have to be challenged in all decision-making processes. Equal
and equitable treatment and participation of women in the correctional
system helps to promote diversity and inclusiveness and a safe environment.

49 
• E
mergencies in Prison Administration : Emergency preparedness is
crucially important for every correctional institution. Establishing a
comprehensive system of emergency preparation and emergency response
requires budget, time, equipment, inter -agency coordination and long-ter
m
m
anagement attention.
• D
ynamic and Static Security in Prisons : prison officers must hav e
kn
owledge and skill training related to physical, procedural and dynamic
security for effective management of Prisons. There is a need to equip the
prison officers with latest tools and technology to face the new challenges.
• Classification of Prisoners: Categorization and classification of prisoners is
very much essential to prevent indiscipline, riots, strikes, attacks, escapes,
and other security related issues in the Prisons. It is also necessary to ensure
special care of vulnerable groups as well as to ensure correctional services to
facilitate rehabilitation and reintegration of prisoners.
• Technology: It is of vital importance to implement various technological
interventions for the purpose of correctional administration. It provides a
structure plan for monitoring the all- round activities in prisons, related to
prison staff, safe and secure custody of prisoners, record keeping etc. and
provides feedback on the attributes that need training, so that there is an
improvement in their respective performance.

Steps taken by Bihar Prisons to address HIV within prisons are as follows: 
Comprehensive health screening of the incoming inmates (within 48 hours of admission) facilitates the 
early detection of HIV -positive individuals. Subsequent to identification, a process of comprehensive and 
accurate diagnosis ensues, ensuring that appropriate treatment modalities are promptly administered to 
incarcerated individuals requiring medical intervention. 
2. Education and Prevention Programs: Inmates are educated on the importance of adopting preventive
measures and seeking timely medical intervention. Through these educational endeavours, incarcerated
populations are equipped with the requisite knowledge and skills to mitigate the risk of HIV acquisition and
transmission.
3. Continuous Monitoring: In addition to stringent regulations, continuous monitoring and evaluation of
H
IV prevalence rates within correctional institutions are conducted to discern emerging patterns and enact
tailored interventions. This monitoring process encompasses assessments conducted both at the prison level
and centrally at headquarters, ensuring a comprehensive oversight of HIV dynamics within correctional
systems.
4. Collaboration with Health Agencies: Collaboration with health agencies and NGOs like YRG Care and
Plan India under BSACS (Bihar State AIDS Control Society), Bihar, Patna constitutes a concerted effort by
correctional authorities to forge partnerships with external healthcare entities. This facilitates enhanced
access to specialized medical care and comprehensive su pport services tailored to meet the unique needs of
HIV-positive inmates within correctional settings.

ormregardingpossessionofthe articles.

space.

 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, 
having been authorized by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, do hereby present this Two 
Hundred Fifty Second Report on Demands for Grants (2025-26) relating to the Ministry of Home 
Affairs (MHA). 
2. Under Rule 272 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States, the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs is mandated to consider the 
Demands for Grants of the related Ministries and make report thereon. In pursuance thereof, the 
Committee in its meetings held on 20th and 21st February, 2025 heard the Home Secretary and other 
officers and considered the Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry of Home Affairs.  
3. The Committee in its sitting held on 6th  March, 2025 considered and adopted the Report.

CHAPTER-I 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1.1. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is responsible for internal security, border 
management, Centre-State relations, administration of Union Territories, management of Central 
Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), Disaster Management, etc. While discharging its duties, the Ministry 
of Home Affairs continuously monitors the internal security situation, issues appropriate advisories, 
shares intelligence inputs, extends manpower and financial support, guidance and expertise to the 
State Governments for maintenance of security, peace and harmony without encroaching upon the 
constitutional rights of the States.   Though 'Public Order' and 'Police' are the responsibilities of 
States as per the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, Article 355 of the Constitution 
enjoins the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to 
ensure that the Government of every State is carried on in accordance with the provisions of the 
Constitution.  
 
1.2 Goals  and  Objectives 
 
1.2.1 The Outcome Budget (2025-26) of the Ministry of Home Affairs throws light on its goals and 
objectives. The MHA administers and implements a wide arch of schemes and programmes as 
mentioned therein in detail.  In brief, the goals and objectives of the Ministry for the year (2025-26) 
are as follows:- 
 
(i) Continuous monitoring of  internal security situation and issuing timely 
advisories; 
(ii) Implementing a zero-tolerance policy against terrorism and drug trafficking; 
(iii) Strengthening border management strategies to enhance national security; 
(iv) Promoting the modernization of the criminal justice system through new laws and 
digitization; 
(v) Enhancing forensic science capabilities to improve the quality of investigations; 
(vi) Developing an Inter-operable Criminal Justice System (ICJS) to facilitate 
seamless  communication between law enforcement agencies; 
(vii) Supporting disaster management initiatives to enhance preparedness and response 
capabilities; 
(viii) Fostering community engagement programs to promote peace, harmony and 
social cohesion; 
(ix) Implementing initiatives for women's safety and empowerment to ensure a secure 
environment for women; 
(x) Timely disbursement of funds for freedom fighters and their families; 
(xi) Ensuring the provision of security, administrative and residential infrastructure of 
CAPFs; 
(xii) Ensuring security and administrative infrastructure for Central Forensic Science 
Laboratories (CFSLs); 
(xiii) Enhancing training, capacity-building and skill development programs for police 
personnel to improve their skills and efficiency; 
(xiv) Supporting the holistic development of islands in Union Territories to enhance 
local governance and infrastructure; 

2 
 
 
(xv) Conducting regular census and surveys to maintain accurate demographic data 
and support policy formulation; 
(xvi) Reimbursement of expenditure under Security Related Expenditure (SRE) to 
States; 
(xvii) Special Infrastructure Support for Left Wing Extremism (LWE) affected States; 
(xviii) Fostering international cooperation on security issues, including counter-terrorism 
and transnational crime; 
(xix) Establishment of a Bhartiya Bhasha Anubhag to support translation services and 
promote linguistic diversity; 
(xx) Scheme for support to poor prisoners; 
(xxi) Modernization of prisons; and 
(xxii) Streamlining immigration processes through the Immigration, Visa, 
Foreigners Registration and Tracking (IVFRT) system.

CHAPTER-II 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2025-26) OF THE MHA 
 
2.1 OVERVIEW 
 
2.1.1 There are eleven Demands for Grants which are administered by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs (MHA). The detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs are divided into 
three volumes: Vol. I, Vol. II-A and Vol. II-B. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volume-I) 
contains three Grants (Nos. 49-51), namely the Ministry of Home Affairs (Grant No. 49); the 
Cabinet (Grant No. 50); and the Police (Grant No. 51). 
 
2.1.2. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volumes-II-A and II-B) relate to the five Union Territories 
(without Legislature), namely Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Grant No. 52), Chandigarh (Grant 
No.53), Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu (Grant No. 54), Ladakh (Grant No. 55) and 
Lakshadweep (Grant No. 56), and three Union Territories (with Legislature), namely Delhi (Grant 
No. 57- Transfers to Delhi), Jammu & Kashmir (Grant No.58- Transfers to Jammu & Kashmir) and 
Puducherry (Grant No. 59- Transfers to Puducherry). 
 
2.1.3 The provisions for the Union Territories (without Legislature) form part of the Demands of 
the Ministry of Home Affairs. However, various programmes/schemes are the subject matter of 
different Ministries, which are responsible for scrutinizing, sanctioning and implementing the 
schemes/projects falling under their respective purview. Provisions for the Union Territories (with a 
Legislature) cover Assistance to the Union Territories of Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir and NCT 
of Delhi, in the form of the Grants and Loans. In respect of these three Grants, the Ministry of Home 
Affairs releases the Grants on quarterly basis and has a limited role in scrutinizing, sanctioning and 
implementation of the schemes/projects.

2.5.3 The Committee observes, based on the above-mentioned information, that the actual 
Budget Estimate (BE) for 2025-26 is lower than the projected BE for 2025-26 across several 
key areas, reflecting a more conservative allocation than initially anticipated. The total budget 
has been reduced from ₹184,236.94 crores (projected BE 2025-26) to ₹160391.06 crores (actual 
BE 2025-26), marking a 12.94% decrease. Within the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), 
actual allocations fall short of projections, with reductions observed across the CRPF, NSG, 
BSF, ITBP, CISF, Assam Rifles, and SSB. This indicates a recalibration of expenditure 
priorities. Similarly, significant downward revisions have been made to allocations for the 
Intelligence Bureau (IB), NATGRID, Central Police Organizations (CPOs) and Delhi Police. 
Police infrastructure projects, particularly CAPF building projects, have experienced a

substantial reduction from ₹6,403.02 crores to ₹4,038.70 crores, which may potentially impact 
construction of new buildings. The Committee notes that such reductions may adversely affect 
critical schemes under these heads and may slow down modernization programs as well as 
hinder the execution of developmental projects, particularly in border areas. Hence, the 
Committee recommends that the MHA may take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance to 
seek increased allocations under these heads in alignment with their original projections. This 
will ensure that the essential developmental schemes are not affected due to insufficient 
funding. The Committee hopes that funds may be demanded for various developmental and 
expansion projects at the RE stage depending on the utilization pattern. 
 
2.5.4 The Committee observes that the significant reduction in the Grant-in-Aid to States for 
Home Guards from ₹ 566.01 crores in RE 2024-25 to ₹30.01 crores in BE 2025-26 is based on 
the expectation that all backlog claims will be cleared in FY 2024-25. However, the Committee 
emphasizes the need to reassess the funding requirements for new claims and ensure that 
States are adequately supported to maintain the operational efficiency of Home Guards. 
Similarly, with respect to the Holistic Development of Islands in Union Territories, where the 
allocation has been reduced from ₹ 88 crores in RE 2024-25 to a nominal ₹0.01 crore in BE 
2025-26, the Committee recommends expediting the preparation of EFC papers and project 
reports to ensure timely approval and funding for developmental activities in the UTs. The 
Committee further recommends closely monitoring expenditure trends and engaging with 
stakeholders to ensure that reductions across various components do not adversely impact 
service delivery or developmental goals. 
 
2.5.5 The Committee recommends the Ministry to take effective measures to address this 
issue by setting clear quarterly targets for fund utilization, enhancing planning and monitoring 
mechanisms to track progress and identifying bottlenecks in project execution at an early 
stage. The Ministry should also consider establishing a reporting mechanism to monitor 
monthly fund utilization and take corrective action wherever delays are identified. The 
Committee is of the view that by adopting these measures, the Ministry can ensure that 
allocated funds are utilized efficiently and effectively throughout the year, thereby avoiding 
last-minute spending rushes and ensuring that the major projects are executed as planned 
without any delay.
