procurement of prison security equipment such as Do or Frame Metal Detectors, baggage 
scanners and frisking equipment; upgradation of vid eo-conferencing infrastructure; and 
implementation of correctional programmes, including vocational training for inmates. 
4.15.2 The Ministry informed that the allocation wa s reduced in RE 2025-26 because progress 
of the Modernization of Prisons Project was affecte d in some States/UTs due to various reasons 
such as delay in finalisation of tender due to court case in Karnataka, site-related constraints such 
as low-lying land requiring land filling work in As sam and delay in finalisation of tender in NCT 
of Delhi. These issues have now been addressed and construction work has started in Assam, 
Karnataka and NCT of Delhi has also completed the t ender process and issued work order on 
05.02.2026. The Project, particularly the establish ment of High Security Prisons, is of national 
importance as it strengthens secure custody of hard ened and high-risk offenders and supports the 
broader internal security framework. Accordingly, a dequate financial provision will be required 
in FY 2026-27 for completion of the construction wo rk of the HSPs in 6 States/UT and 
upgradation of security infrastructure in prisons a cross the country. The outcomes of the Project 
are being monitored through regular review of physi cal and financial progress by States/UTs. 
Progress of High Security Prison work, deployment of security equipment and implementation of 
correctional programmes are the key indicators for assessing improvements in prison safety, 
infrastructure and rehabilitation. 
4.15.3 The Committee was also apprised that while t he Modernization of Prisons Project does 
not provide for upgradation of existing prisons or establishment of open jails, it contributes to 
better prison management through strengthening of s ecurity infrastructure and correctional 

69 
 
administration. The Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act is a prison reform initiative and 
States and UTs are being continuously encouraged to  adopt the Model Act in their respective 
jurisdictions. The allocation under the Project wil l therefore be utilised on completion of High 
Security Prisons and organisation of correctional p rogrammes, including vocational training for 
inmates, aimed at improving prison security, management and rehabilitation outcomes. 
Observation / Recommendation 
4.15.4 
 The Committee notes that the Modernization of Priso ns Project primarily focuses 
on establishment of High Security Prisons and stren gthening of security infrastructure. 
While secure custody of high-risk offenders is esse ntial, the Committee observes that issues 
relating to overcrowding, ageing infrastructure and  living conditions in existing prisons 
remain areas of concern.  
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may exam ine the feasibility of 
extending modernization support to upgradation of e xisting prison infrastructure, 
including improvement of sanitation, healthcare fac ilities, digital record management and 
segregation facilities, in consultation with States /UTs. A balanced approach addressing 
both security and humane custodial conditions would  strengthen overall prison 
administration and internal security objectives. 
4.15.5 The Committee notes that a substantial propo rtion of the prison population 
comprises undertrial prisoners. The Committee, ther efore, recommends that appropriate 
segregation between undertrial and convicted prison ers may be ensured in prisons, in 
accordance with established legal and correctional principles. While undertaking prison 
modernization, States/UTs may consider prioritising infrastructure planning that facilitates 
separate accommodation and suitable custodial arran gements for these categories so that 
such measures would help safeguard the rights of un dertrial prisoners, reduce the risk of 
negative influence of convicted criminals and contr ibute to better prison management and 
discipline. 
4.16 SUPPORT TO POOR PRISONERS 
4.16.1 The Committee sought details regarding the n umber of prisoners benefitted under the 
Support to Poor Prisoners Scheme, the average proce ssing time for assistance and challenges 
encountered in timely delivery of support. The Mini stry informed that since inception of the 
Scheme, 262 prisoners have been provided financial assistance. It was further stated that the 
Guidelines and Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) o f the Scheme have recently been revised 
to ensure time-bound and effective implementation. 
4.16.2 As per the revised SOP, cases of undertrial prisoners who are not released within seven 
days of grant of bail are required to be reported b y Jail Authorities to the concerned District 
Legal Services Authority (DLSA). Verification and i nteraction by Jail Visiting 

70 
 
Lawyers/Paralegal Volunteers is to be completed wit hin five days. Thereafter, the cases are 
placed before the District Level Empowered Committe e, which is mandated to meet twice a 
month (on the 1st and 3rd Mondays of each month or the next working day) to consider eligible 
cases. The Committee is required to take a decision  and ensure availability of funds to the Court 
within a further five days. The Ministry stated tha t these clearly defined timelines are intended to 
minimise delays and procedural bottlenecks in extending assistance. 
4.16.3 With regard to challenges in timely delivery  of support, the Ministry informed that 
several States/UTs have reported that a significant  number of prisoners are not eligible under the 
Scheme due to their involvement in multiple cases o r in heinous offences such as terrorism-
related offences, offences affecting national secur ity, dowry death, rape, human trafficking and 
offences under the POCSO Act, NDPS Act, Unlawful Ac tivities (Prevention) Act, Prevention of 
Corruption Act and Prevention of Money Laundering A ct, for which benefits under the Scheme 
are not admissible. 
Observation / Recommendation 
 
4.16.4 The Committee notes that while the Support t o Poor Prisoners Scheme provides 
important financial assistance to undertrial prison ers who are unable to furnish bail, the 
number of beneficiaries since inception remains lim ited. The Committee appreciates the 
revision of Guidelines and Standard Operating Proce dure to ensure defined timelines at 
each stage of processing. The Committee recommends that greater awareness regarding 
the Scheme may be generated among prison authoritie s, legal aid institutions and eligible 
prisoners to ensure that deserving beneficiaries are not left out due to lack of information. 
 
4.17 VIBRANT VILLAGES PROGRAMME 
4.17.1 The Ministry has informed the Committee that  Vibrant Village Programme is for 
comprehensive development in phased manner of selec ted border villages. This includes village 
infrastructure development, road connectivity and o ther developmental works. The Ministry also 
informed that the Vibrant Villages Programme-II foc uses on improving living conditions and 
livelihoods in selected border villages. Its core a reas include village infrastructure, road and 
telecom connectivity, electrification, basic servic es, livelihood support, and integration of border 
populations with the nation. 
Vibrant Villages Programme–I 
4.17.2 The Committee was informed that the Vibrant Villages Programme (VVP) was launched 
with the objective of enhancing vibrancy in border villages and reversing outmigration by 
providing adequate incentives and improving living conditions. The Programme covers 662 
villages across 4 States and 1 Union Territory, wit h an approximate population coverage of 1.5 
lakh persons. The financial outlay for FY 2023–26 i s ₹4,800 crores, including the road 

71 
 
component, with an additional allocation of ₹440.82  crores for construction of Long Span 
Bridges (LSBs). 
4.17.3 The Ministry informed that since its launch in Kibithoo, Anjaw district, Arunachal 
Pradesh in 2023, several outreach and development a ctivities have been undertaken. Seventeen 
Union Cabinet Ministers have visited 34 VVP villages across 8 districts, and 92 officials from 17 
Ministries have visited 259 villages. More than 8,5 00 activities have been organized in the 
identified villages. Under VVP-I, 263 projects amounting to ₹116 crore have been sanctioned for 
development of tourism infrastructure. In addition,  112 road works amounting to ₹2,513 crore 
have been approved. A total of 2,663 projects worth  ₹1,172 crore have been sanctioned by the 
Ministry of Home Affairs under VVP-I and through co nvergence with Central Ministries and 
Departments for comprehensive development of these villages. The Programme aims to 
strengthen socio-economic resilience, prevent borde r depopulation and reinforce the first line of 
defence through community development initiatives. 
Vibrant Villages Programme–II (VVP-II) 
4.17.4 The Committee was further informed that Vibr ant Villages Programme–II has been 
approved as a Central Sector Scheme with effect from April 2025, with a total financial outlay of 
₹6,839 crores for the period FY 2024–29. VVP-II cov ers 1,954 villages across approximately 
100 districts in 17 States and Union Territories lo cated along land borders other than the 
Northern Border already covered under VVP-I. 
4.17.5 The objectives of VVP-II include strengtheni ng internal security by assimilating border 
populations with the national mainstream and encour aging their role as the “eyes and ears” of 
border guarding forces; improving living conditions  and livelihood opportunities; and weaning 
communities away from inimical activities while controlling trans-border crime. 
4.17.6 The strategy under VVP-II includes saturatio n of villages abutting International Land 
Borders (ILBs) with connectivity infrastructure suc h as telecom, roads, power and television; 
creation of diverse and sustainable livelihood oppo rtunities; development of infrastructure 
including education and tourism; and undertaking bo rder-specific outreach activities. The 
Programme seeks to enhance socio-economic developme nt, improve connectivity and 
infrastructure and reinforce community participatio n in national security objectives in border 
areas. 
Observation / Recommendation 
4.17.7 The Committee appreciates the Vibrant Villag es Programme (VVP) as a significant 
initiative aimed at comprehensive development of bo rder villages through phased 
infrastructure augmentation, livelihood generation and enhanced connectivity. The 
Committee notes that VVP-I has led to substantial p rogress in road connectivity, tourism 
infrastructure and convergence-based developmental activities and that VVP-II expands 
the scope of coverage to additional border regions.  The Programme’s emphasis on socio-

72 
 
economic resilience, prevention of outmigration and  integration of border populations with 
the national mainstream is commendable and aligns w ith broader national security 
objectives. The Committee recommends that livelihoo d initiatives under VVP-II be closely 
aligned with local geographic and cultural strength s, including promotion of border 
tourism, agro-based industries, handicrafts and eco -tourism. Skill development 
programmes tailored to local conditions may be inte grated with market linkages to ensure 
sustainable income generation. Enhanced coordinatio n with Border Guarding Forces and 
community institutions may also be incorporated to strengthen participatory security and 
foster a sense of shared responsibility in border management.

5.2.5  Andaman and Nicobar Islands constitute the l argest archipelago system in the Bay of

connected to the mainland primarily through air and  water routes. The Committee took note of 
the increased tourism activity in the region and en quired about the steps taken to augment air

recommends that larger aircraft may be deployed on these routes to increase passenger 
capacity and help reduce airfares. Early operationa lisation of the approved seaplane 
services under the UDAN scheme may be ensured to im prove last-mile connectivity to 
remote islands of the Union Territory. Appropriate fare rationalisation measures may be 
explored so that air travel remains affordable for residents and tourists.  
 
TOURISM 
 
5.2.9 Tourism development plays a crucial role in t he economic, social and cultural growth of 
the Union territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.  Due to its natural beauty, biodiversity and 
strategic location, tourism is one of the most impo rtant sectors for the islands’ development. It 
has vast potential of generating revenue for the is lands. It creates direct employment in hotels, 
tour operators and transport services. At the same time, it creates avenues for fisheries, 
handicrafts, local markets and can encourage entrepreneurship among local population. 
 
5.2.10 The Committee noted with interest the sharp rise in tourist arrivals in the Andaman and 
Nicobar Islands, increasing from 7.22 lakh in 2024 to 8.23 lakh in 2025. The Administration 
informed that five major resort projects under the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) mode have 
been successfully bid out, drawing strong market re sponse from reputed international hospitality 
groups. The Committee further noted the proposal to  open eleven uninhabited islands for 

79 
 
regulated day-tourism in coordination with the Fore st Department. While welcoming these 
initiatives aimed at enhancing tourism infrastructure and revenue, the Committee emphasized the 
importance of maintaining world-class standards consistent with global eco-tourism benchmarks.  
 
Observation / Recommendation 
 
5.2.11 The Committee recommends that PPP tourism pr ojects adhere to internationally 
recognised environmental and construction norms. Co mprehensive environmental impact 
assessments and carrying-capacity studies may be co nducted prior to project 
implementation. Provisions for local employment gen eration and skill development may be 
incorporated in the agreements so that the local po pulation benefits from tourism 
development. A robust monitoring mechanism may be i nstituted to ensure that ecological 
sustainability is not compromised in the expansion of tourism activities. 
 
5.2.12 The Committee recommends that the impact of development in tourism sector on 
revenue generation in the UT and on the socio econo mic growth of the local population of 
the A&N Islands may be assessed. The benefits of ec onomic growth in the UT must also 
percolate to the local population as they equally d eserve to reap those benefits. The 
Committee recommends that the UT Administration exp lore opportunities for developing 
tourism-related activities in islands that are pres ently uninhabited but have scenic beaches 
and potential for eco-tourism, and develop them as tourist destinations for the growing 
number of visitors to the UT.

Committee was informed that the UT Administration h as established Emergency Operation

television, radio, social media, sirens, megaphones  and mobile-based systems such as SMS

INCOIS, with centralised activation at the Director ate of Disaster Management, Sri Vijaya 
Puram. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
5.2.18 The Committee observes that timely dissemina tion of early warnings and 
community preparedness of disaster management are c ritical in an island territory 
where evacuation windows are limited. The Committee  recommends expansion of 
automated siren coverage to all vulnerable coastal locations, periodic audit of 
dissemination response time across communication ch annels and establishment of 
maintenance protocols for warning infrastructure. R egular mock drills and capacity-
building programmes may continue to ensure sustained preparedness.

ROAD CONNECTIVITY 
 
5.2.36 The Committee noted that under the current g uidelines of the Pradhan Mantri Gram 
Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), road connectivity under PMGSY  is generally provided to habitations 
with a minimum population of 250 persons. However, The UT administration brought to the 
Committee’s attention during meeting that approxima tely 60 habitations in the Andaman and 
Nicobar Islands fall below this threshold, with pop ulation clusters ranging between 100 to 150 
persons. These habitations, many of which are located in tribal and geographically isolated areas, 
continue to face acute connectivity challenges. The  Committee also observed that such a 
constraint is not unique to the Andaman and Nicobar  Islands, but is also relevant to other Union 
Territories with sparsely populated settlements such as Ladakh. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
5.2.37 The Committee recommends that the Ministry o f Home Affairs may pursue this 
matter with the Ministry of Rural Development that it may examine the feasibility of 
relaxing the existing population norms under PMGSY for islands’ territories and other 
similarly placed regions. A dedicated flexi-provisi on may be incorporated in the scheme to 
allow inclusion of habitations that are critically in need of road connectivity despite having 
population below the threshold.

HEALTH 
 
5.5.4 The Committee sought detailed information reg arding the steps being taken to improve 
healthcare access in remote and difficult areas of the Union Territory of Ladakh, particularly with 
regard to strengthening of infrastructure, availabi lity of medical personnel and emergency 
response mechanisms. 
 
5.5.5 The Ministry, in its reply, informed that sig nificant measures have been undertaken to 
enhance healthcare access across the geographically challenging terrain of Ladakh.  
1.
 Health Care Infrastructure 
 Ladakh has District Hospitals at the district level , Community Health Centres (CHCs) 
and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) at the block leve l and Ayushman Arogya Mandir-
Sub Health Centres (AAM-SHCs) at the village level,  with a total of 335 health 
facilities. 
 All 32 Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and 288 Sub-Health Centres (SHCs) in the Union 
Territory have been upgraded to Ayushman Arogya Man dirs (AAMs) under the 
Ayushman Bharat initiative.  
 These facilities deliver services across 12 identif ied service domains. District Hospitals 
function as referral units and cater to all medical emergencies.  
 Medical camps are conducted regularly in the remote st and hard-to-reach areas. 
Essential drugs and a defined package of diagnostic  tests are provided free of cost at all 
levels to ensure timely diagnosis and treatment. 
 
2.
 Medical Staff Availability 
 Ayushman Arogya Mandirs are staffed with essential human resources, including 288 
Community Health Officers (CHOs) at SHCs and one Me dical Officer at each PHC, 
supported by 651 ASHAs and 555 ANMs, to deliver com prehensive clinical and public 
health services. 
 In addition, the following medical personnel are in position across the Union Territory: 
o 98 Specialist Consultants and 01 Super-Specialist 
o 169 Medical Officers 
o 35 Dental Surgeons 
o 45 AYUSH Doctors 
3. Emergency Services 

96 
 
 A structured referral and follow-up mechanism is in  place between SHCs, PHCs, CHCs 
and District Hospitals to ensure timely referrals, especially for emergencies and chronic 
conditions in remote and hard-to-reach areas of Ladakh. 
 To enhance healthcare accessibility in high-risk zo nes, 27 ambulance stations with 108 
ambulance services are strategically positioned acr oss Ladakh to enable rapid 
emergency response. Tele-medicine services are also  operational, extending healthcare 
services up to the village level. 
 
5.5.6 The Committee also sought information regardi ng the effective implementation of 
Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY in Ladakh and the challenges faced therein. The Ministry informed 
that Universal Health Coverage (UHC) was launched i n convergence with PM-JAY in December 
2020 to ensure coverage of remaining families. At p resent, 12,120 families are covered under 
AB-PMJAY, fully sponsored by the Government of Indi a. Outreach initiatives such as 
“AapkeDwar Ayushman” and Health Mela campaigns have  been conducted in remote areas 
including Nubra, Zanskar, Nyoma, Hanle, Chumathang,  Drass and Batalik to enhance awareness 
and facilitate enrolment. Internal block-wise and t ehsil-wise targets have been fixed for issuance 
of Ayushman Golden Cards to enable access to cashle ss treatment. In view of the absence of a 
tertiary care centre in Ladakh, the UT Administrati on provides travel expense support to 
beneficiaries referred outside the UT for advanced treatment. 
 
5.5.7 Further, with regard to budgetary allocation,  the Committee noted that ₹68.44 crores has 
been provided under Medical and Public Health in BE  2026-27. The Ministry informed that 
₹67.19 crores of this allocation pertains to the re venue component, primarily for heating charges 
of District Hospitals, PHCs, CHCs and GNM School an d for procurement of medical supplies 
and essential drugs. An amount of ₹1.25 crores unde r the capital component is earmarked for 
completion of ongoing works at SNM Hospital, Leh an d Sub-District Hospital, Drass. The 
Ministry further stated that additional funds, if r equired, would be projected at the Revised 
Estimates stage. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
5.5.8 The Committee appreciates the efforts made to  strengthen healthcare delivery in 
the remote and high-altitude regions of Ladakh, inc luding upgradation of PHCs and Sub-
Health Centres into Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, deploy ment of medical personnel, 
operationalisation of tele-medicine services and es tablishment of structured referral 
mechanisms. However, the Committee observes that La dakh continues to face unique 
geographical and climatic challenges which directly  impact healthcare delivery. The 
absence of a tertiary care centre within the Union Territory compels patients to travel 
outside the UT for advanced treatment. While travel  assistance is being provided, such 
referrals may cause delay in critical care, particu larly during winter months when 
connectivity is severely affected. 
 

97 
 
5.5.9 The Committee further notes that a substantia l portion of the allocation under 
Medical and Public Health for 2026-27 is towards re venue expenditure, including heating 
charges and procurement of essential supplies, whil e the capital component remains 
limited. Considering the strategic and sensitive lo cation of the UT and its dispersed 
population, strengthening of permanent health infrastructure assumes special importance. 
 
5.5.10 The Committee recommends that the feasibilit y of establishing tertiary-level 
healthcare facilities in Ladakh may be examined on priority so as to reduce dependence on 
referrals outside the UT. Availability of specialis t and super-specialist may be strengthened 
through incentive-based postings, rotational deputa tions or tele-specialist support. Capital 
investment in critical health infrastructure, parti cularly in District Hospitals and 
emergency care facilities, may be enhanced in a pha sed manner. Emergency response 
systems may be further strengthened keeping in view  extreme weather conditions and 
accessibility constraints. Implementation of Ayushm an Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan 
Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) and Universal Health Coverag e (UHC) may be periodically 
reviewed to ensure universal coverage and timely se ttlement of claims.  Sustained and 
focused attention to healthcare in Ladakh remains e ssential in view of its terrain, climatic 
conditions and strategic importance.

WATER SUPPLY, SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 
 
5.5.26 The Committee noted that the allocation for Water Supply and Sanitation has declined 
from ₹11.30 crores in RE 2025-26 to ₹9.80 crores in  BE 2026-27. The Committee sought to 
know how the UT Administration proposes to address drinking water scarcity and sanitation 
challenges in remote and high-altitude habitations in view of the reduced allocation. 
 
5.5.27 The Ministry, in its reply, informed that th e reduction under this head is primarily on 
account of Fuels and Lubricants. The enhanced provi sions in RE 2025-26 were made to clear 
pending liabilities of the previous year. The alloc ations in BE 2026-27 have been rationalized in 
order to adhere to the revenue and capital expendit ure ceilings prescribed by the Ministry of 
Finance. 
 
5.5.28 It was further informed that the allocation under this head is largely utilized for revenue 
expenditure towards fuels and lubricants for water tankers, procurement of water-supply-related 
spare parts and stores, repair and maintenance of w ater supply schemes and tankers and payment 
of electricity dues for water lifting points. 
 
5.5.29 To address drinking water supply and sanitat ion requirements in remote and high-altitude 
habitations, the Ministry stated that any additiona l requirements will be met, as far as feasible, 
from the Tribal Area Component. Further, initiative s under Central Sponsored Schemes such as 
Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) and AMRUT are being implem ented. Accordingly, drinking water 
supply and sanitation requirements will be addresse d through coordinated funding and 
implementation by the UT and CSS schemes in synergy. 
 
5.5.30 With regard to sustainable water management,  the Ministry informed that the 
Administration of the Union Territory of Ladakh is addressing water supply challenges and 
ensuring sustainable water resource management thro ugh a comprehensive, climate-resilient and 
institutionally coordinated approach, keeping in vi ew the region’s low rainfall, cold desert 
ecology and increasing impacts of climate change. 
 
 Under the Jal Jeevan Mission, the UT Administration , through the District Water & 
Sanitation Missions (DWSMs), is implementing measur es for planning, execution, 
monitoring and long-term sustainability of drinking water schemes.  
 The DWSMs play a pivotal role in district-level con vergence, source sustainability 
planning, monitoring of scheme performance and stre ngthening community institutions, 

102 
 
particularly Village Water & Sanitation Committees (VWSCs). 
 Sustainable water supply is being ensured through i dentification, protection and 
augmentation of reliable sources such as springs, g laciers, snow-fed streams and 
groundwater, supported by spring-shed management, c atchment area treatment and 
recharge interventions.  
 In view of climate variability and declining snowfa ll, the Administration, under the 
guidance of DWSMs, is promoting storage-based solut ions, including construction of 
reservoirs, winter water harvesting systems and ado ption of locally appropriate 
innovations such as artificial glaciers and ice stupas, which help store excess winter water 
for summer use. 
 The DWSMs are also responsible for regular water qu ality monitoring and surveillance, 
ensuring compliance with national drinking water qu ality standards through laboratory 
testing, field-level inspections and community-base d water quality monitoring. Capacity 
building of local manpower for operation and mainte nance, promotion of water 
conservation practices and community ownership of assets are being actively pursued. 
 Further, the Administration is ensuring inter-secto ral convergence at the district level 
through DWSMs with schemes related to watershed dev elopment, afforestation, rural 
livelihoods and climate adaptation, thereby strengt hening the resilience of drinking water 
systems in Ladakh’s fragile Himalayan ecosystem. 
 
5.5.31 Through these coordinated institutional and technical interventions, the Administration 
aims to ensure safe, adequate and sustainable drink ing water supply, while enhancing long-term 
resilience against climate change impacts in the Union Territory of Ladakh.

strengthening Solid Waste Management infrastructure  in Leh and for establishment of a 
Sewage Treatment Plant in Kargil. 
 
5.5.39 The Committee observes that Ladakh’s fragile  ecosystem, high-altitude terrain, low 
rainfall and increasing tourism and urbanisation pr essures require sustained and forward-
looking investment in drinking water supply, sanita tion and scientific management of solid 
and liquid waste.  
 
5.5.40 The Committee recommends that drinking water  security and source sustainability 
be treated as priority areas, with focused capital investment in storage, recharge and 
climate-resilient infrastructure. Proposals submitt ed under SBM-Urban 2.0 for 
strengthening Solid Waste Management and Used Water  Management be expedited for 
early approval and time-bound implementation. Decen tralised waste processing, safe 
landfill practices, operationalisation of the propo sed Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) at 
Kargil and strict monitoring of water quality and w aste disposal systems be ensured. An 
integrated and climate-resilient approach combining  water supply, sanitation and waste 
management be adopted to safeguard Ladakh’s fragile  Himalayan environment while 
meeting the needs of remote and tribal habitations.

5.6.10 Urban development and basic civic infrastruc ture remain critical sectors for the Union 
Territory of Lakshadweep in view of its limited lan d availability, fragile coastal ecosystem and 
vulnerability to climate-related risks. Allocation under Urban Development, Housing, Water 
Supply and Flood Control has been ₹61.28 crores in BE 2026-27.  
5.6.11 With regard to water security, the Ministry has informed that the UT continues to rely 
significantly on desalination technologies, includi ng Low Temperature Thermal Desalination 
(LTTD) plants, in addition to rainwater harvesting systems. The Ministry has informed that 
ongoing projects aim at ensuring year-round availab ility of potable water across inhabited 
islands. Funds are also being utilised for maintena nce and upgradation of existing distribution 
networks to reduce transmission losses. Further, de salination plants have been installed in all 
islands, except Andrott, where the Low Temperature Thermal Desalination plant (LTTD) is 
expected to be completed by April, 2026.  
 
5.6.12 Further, in the area of coastal protection a nd flood control, scientific shoreline 
management plans have been prepared in consultation  with expert agencies. Anti-sea erosion 
measures are being addressed through scientific sho reline management plans prepared by 

111 
 
National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM), following the discontinuation 
of hard coastal structures as per Ministry of Envir onment, Forest and Climate Change 
(MoEFCC) directions. Diaphragm walls along peripher al roads are currently proposed to protect 
land and infrastructure from wave action and erosion. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
5.6.13 The Committee observes that in small island territories, urban development and 
water supply are directly linked to public health, tourism sustainability and environmental 
stability. Any delay in desalination or drainage pr ojects can have immediate consequences 
on quality of life and economic activity. The Commi ttee notes that the success of urban 
development interventions in Lakshadweep depends on  sustainable planning, strict 
adherence to Coastal Regulation Zone norms and time ly completion of projects. Water 
security measures, particularly desalination, requi re continuous technical supervision and 
maintenance.  
5.6.14 The Committee recommends that ongoing desali nation and water augmentation 
projects be completed in a time-bound manner and th at regular monitoring of water 
quality and supply hours be managed properly. Urban  drainage and flood mitigation 
works may be prioritised in vulnerable islands to a ddress climate-related risks. Coastal 
protection projects may comply with environmental s afeguards and adopt eco-sensitive 
methods. Periodic reporting on physical and financi al progress of urban infrastructure 
projects may also be placed before the Monitoring a uthority to ensure effective utilisation 
of funds.

Observation/Recommendation 
5.6.29 The Committee notes that power supply in Lak shadweep is predominantly 
dependent on diesel-based power generation due to t he absence of mainland grid 
connectivity. While allocations have been provided for operation and maintenance of 
power stations and for introduction of renewable energy projects, recurring expenditure on 
fuel continues to impose a significant financial bu rden. The Committee also observes that 
logistical constraints and weather-related disrupti ons can affect timely fuel supply, thereby 
impacting reliability of power in the islands.  
5.6.30 The Committee recommends that although steps  have been initiated for solar power 
generation with battery storage systems, the scale of renewable integration requires further 
augmentation to ensure long-term sustainability and  energy security. The UT 
Administration may adopt a phased and time-bound st rategy to progressively reduce 
dependency on diesel-based generation by expanding solar power projects integrated with 
adequate battery energy storage systems. Capital in vestments may be prioritised towards 
strengthening renewable base-load capacity and modernising transmission and distribution 
infrastructure. An island-wise energy transition plan with measurable targets for reduction 
in diesel consumption and improvement in system eff iciency may also be prepared. 
Periodic monitoring of fuel expenditure vis-à-vis  renewable energy generation may be 
considered to ensure fiscal prudence, reliability o f supply and long-term sustainability of 
the power sector in the Union Territory.

Observations /Recommendations  
 
5.8.25  The Committee notes with satisfaction the significa nt growth in tourist arrivals 
from 2022 to 2024, with total footfall increasing f rom 1.88 crores to 2.36 crores. The sharp 
increase in foreign tourist arrivals from about 20, 000 in 2022 to over 65,000 in 2024 is 
particularly noteworthy and reflects growing intern ational confidence in the Union 
Territory as a tourist destination. 

130 
 
 
5.8.26 The Committee further observes that although  there was a decline in tourist 
arrivals in 2025 compared to 2024, largely attributable to the Pahalgam incident, the sector 
demonstrates resilience with recovery visible from June 2025 onwards. The cumulative 
footfall of approximately 1.78 crores by December 2 025 indicates restoration of confidence 
and sustained interest among visitors. 
 
5.8.27 The Committee is of the view that tourism co ntinues to be one of the key drivers of 
economic activity and employment generation in the Union Territory. The upward trend in 
tourist arrivals during recent years has contribute d significantly to livelihoods in 
hospitality, transport, handicrafts and allied sect ors. With regard to development of new 
destinations, the Committee notes the allocation of  ₹26.24 crores under the State Capex 
Budget and ₹20.33 crores under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme for development of 
infrastructure at Kokernag, Bhaderwah, Doodhpathri and adjoining areas. The Committee 
appreciates the efforts made to diversify tourism b eyond traditional hubs such as Srinagar, 
Gulmarg and Pahalgam. 
 
5.8.28 The Committee observes that sustained growth  in tourist footfall necessitates 
comprehensive planning to avoid over-concentration and ecological stress in popular 
destinations. The Committee recommends that develop ment of emerging destinations must 
be accompanied by adequate infrastructure, waste ma nagement systems, carrying capacity 
assessment, connectivity improvement and local comm unity participation. A long-term 
sustainable tourism strategy be prepared integratin g environmental safeguards and 
tourists carrying capacity norms. Infrastructure de velopment initiatives at emerging 
destinations may be expedited in a time-bound manner with clear outcome indicators.  
 
5.8.29 The Committee further recommends greater emp hasis may be placed on high-value 
tourism segments such as eco-tourism, adventure tou rism and winter tourism. Skill 
development and entrepreneurship support may also b e provided to local youth to 
maximise livelihood benefits. Measures for periodic  monitoring of tourist satisfaction, 
safety perception and infrastructure adequacy could be initiated. The Committee reiterates 
that tourism has emerged as a vital sector for econ omic revitalisation of Jammu & 
Kashmir and sustained focus on diversification, inf rastructure strengthening and 
confidence-building measures will be essential to maintain the growth momentum.

DELHI POLICE 
 The Committee notes that increasing representation  of women in police forces is 
essential for promoting gender-sensitive policing, improving public trust and enhancing 
response to crimes against women and vulnerable sec tions. The Committee is of the view 
that Delhi, being the National Capital with a diver se and dense population, requires a 

146 
 
strengthened and balanced force structure reflectin g adequate representation of women 
personnel at all levels.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Minis try, in coordination with 
Delhi Police, may prepare a phased and time-bound r oadmap to enhance the strength of 
women personnel to at least 33 percent of the total  sanctioned strength. Focused 
recruitment drives, adequate training capacity, pro vision of suitable infrastructure 
including separate accommodation and facilities, an d enabling service conditions may be 
ensured to achieve this objective in a sustainable manner. 
(Para 4.8.6) 
 
 The Committee observes that hesitation among citiz ens to visit police stations often 
stems from perceptions of inaccessibility, lack of transparency and discomfort in 
interacting with personnel. Such barriers have pote ntial to discourage reporting of crime, 
weaken community participation and reduce trust in law enforcement.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Delhi Pol ice may adopt a citizen-
centric policing model to make police stations more  approachable, transparent and 
responsive. In this regard, the Ministry and Delhi Police may explore and adopt best 
practices such as establishing dedicated One-Stop Citizen Service Desks at police stations to 
assist visitors with inquiries and reporting proced ures; deploying Community Liaison 
Officers for outreach and follow-up with local comm unities; creating Victim Support 
Corners to provide private and supportive spaces fo r women, children and senior citizens; 
instituting structured feedback and grievance redre ssal mechanisms with defined 
timelines; and prominently displaying service chart ers outlining procedures and rights of 
complainants.  
(Para 4.8.7) 
 The Committee recommends expansion of mobile and c ommunity policing 
initiatives through regular engagement in markets and residential areas, and strengthening 
of online reporting and appointment systems to faci litate access without requiring physical 
visits. Regular training of personnel in communicat ion skills, sensitivity and public 
interface management may also be undertaken, and pe riodic community satisfaction 
surveys may be conducted to assess and improve service delivery. 
(Para 4.8.8) 
 
 The Committee observes that cases relating to miss ing persons, particularly women, 
children and vulnerable individuals, have significa nt social and security implications in a 
metropolitan city like Delhi. The Committee is of t he view that a data-driven and research-
oriented approach is necessary to understand the un derlying socio-economic, demographic 
and behavioural factors contributing to such cases.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Delhi Pol ice may undertake a 
comprehensive sociological study in collaboration w ith reputed universities and research 

147 
 
institutions to analyse patterns and root causes of  missing persons’ cases. The study may 
include comparative analysis of missing rates in De lhi vis-à-vis other metropolitan cities in 
India as well as selected international cities, wit h a view to identifying best practices and 
systemic gaps. The findings of such a study may be utilised for policy formulation, 
preventive strategies, improved tracking mechanisms and community-based interventions. 
(Para 4.8.9) 
 Further, the Committee observes that effective imp lementation of provisions 
relating to plea bargaining under the Bharatiya Nag arik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) can 
play a significant role in reducing pendency of cas es, expediting disposal of minor offences 
and easing the burden on investigating agencies, co urts and correctional institutions. The 
Committee also observes that structured use of plea  bargaining mechanisms may 
contribute to faster resolution of cases, reduced u ndertrial prisoners and improved 
efficiency of the criminal justice system.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Delhi Pol ice may take proactive steps 
to sensitise investigating officers and supervisory  officers regarding the scope and 
procedural requirements of plea bargaining under th e BNSS. Awareness measures may be 
undertaken, in coordination with prosecution and le gal services authorities, to ensure 
informed participation of eligible accused persons.  Periodic review of cases disposed off 
through plea bargaining may also be conducted to as sess its effectiveness in reducing case 
backlog and custodial burden. 
(Para 4.8.10) 
 The Committee, further, notes the increasing deplo yment of CCTV cameras, body-
worn cameras, traffic surveillance systems, IoT-ena bled devices and integrated 
communication platforms by Delhi Police as part of modernization and smart policing 
initiatives. While appreciating the technological a dvancements, the Committee also 
observes that robust data protection and cybersecur ity safeguards are critical to prevent 
misuse, unauthorised access, data breaches and comp romise of sensitive operational 
personal information. The Committee, therefore, rec ommends that Delhi Police may adopt 
a comprehensive data security framework covering en cryption standards, secure data 
storage, controlled access protocols, periodic cybersecurity audits and real-time monitoring 
of surveillance systems. 
(Para 4.8.11) 
 The Committee recommends that private individuals and establishments installing 
CCTV systems may be encouraged or mandated to procu re devices only from 
manufacturers that comply with notified data securi ty, encryption and secure server 
standards. Periodic advisories and awareness campai gns may also be issued to promote 
adoption of secure systems and prevent misuse, hack ing or unauthorised access to 
surveillance data. 
(Para 4.8.12) 

148

 The Committee notes that 62 major traffic congesti on points have been identified

obstruction of roads. The Committee recommends that  Delhi Police, in coordination with

management strategy, including strict enforcement a gainst illegal parking on roads and 
residential areas, promotion of designated parking zones and use of technology-enabled 
parking monitoring systems. The Committee further r ecommends that commercial 
establishments may be mandated to ensure adequate o ff-street parking facilities to reduce 
spill-over onto public roads.

enforcement measures may be explored to ensure comp liance and promote responsible 
road behaviour.

 The Committee also notes instances of motorcycles fitted with modified or non-
standard silencers that produce excessive noise, le ading to sound pollution and causing

149 
 
Delhi Police may strengthen enforcement against suc h violations through regular checking 
drives, strict penalties and coordination with tran sport authorities to ensure compliance 
with prescribed vehicle noise standards.

 The Committee observes that begging at traffic sig nals not only poses safety risks

each stage of processing. The Committee recommends that greater awareness regarding

reduction. Investment in slope stabilisation, embankment strengthening, glacier and GLOF 
monitoring, floodplain management and community-bas ed preparedness will reduce 
recurring expenditure on restoration of damaged infrastructure and compensation . 
 
(Para 5.8.19) 
 

171 
 
TOURISM 
 The Committee notes with satisfaction the significa nt growth in tourist arrivals 
from 2022 to 2024, with total footfall increasing f rom 1.88 crores to 2.36 crores. The sharp 
increase in foreign tourist arrivals from about 20, 000 in 2022 to over 65,000 in 2024 is 
particularly noteworthy and reflects growing intern ational confidence in the Union 
Territory as a tourist destination. 
(Para 5.8.25) 
 
 The Committee further observes that although there  was a decline in tourist 
arrivals in 2025 compared to 2024, largely attributable to the Pahalgam incident, the sector 
demonstrates resilience with recovery visible from June 2025 onwards. The cumulative 
footfall of approximately 1.78 crores by December 2 025 indicates restoration of confidence 
and sustained interest among visitors. 
 
(Para 5.8.26) 
 
 The Committee is of the view that tourism continue s to be one of the key drivers of 
economic activity and employment generation in the Union Territory. The upward trend in 
tourist arrivals during recent years has contribute d significantly to livelihoods in 
hospitality, transport, handicrafts and allied sect ors. With regard to development of new 
destinations, the Committee notes the allocation of  ₹26.24 crores under the State Capex 
Budget and ₹20.33 crores under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme for development of 
infrastructure at Kokernag, Bhaderwah, Doodhpathri and adjoining areas. The Committee 
appreciates the efforts made to diversify tourism b eyond traditional hubs such as Srinagar, 
Gulmarg and Pahalgam. 
 
(Para 5.8.27) 
 
 The Committee observes that sustained growth in to urist footfall necessitates 
comprehensive planning to avoid over-concentration and ecological stress in popular 
destinations. The Committee recommends that develop ment of emerging destinations must 
be accompanied by adequate infrastructure, waste ma nagement systems, carrying capacity 
assessment, connectivity improvement and local comm unity participation. A long-term 
sustainable tourism strategy be prepared integratin g environmental safeguards and 
tourists carrying capacity norms. Infrastructure de velopment initiatives at emerging 
destinations may be expedited in a time-bound manner with clear outcome indicators.  
 
(Para 5.8.28) 
 
 The Committee further recommends greater emphasis may be placed on high-value 
tourism segments such as eco-tourism, adventure tou rism and winter tourism. Skill 

172 
 
development and entrepreneurship support may also b e provided to local youth to 
maximise livelihood benefits. Measures for periodic  monitoring of tourist satisfaction, 
safety perception and infrastructure adequacy could be initiated. The Committee reiterates 
that tourism has emerged as a vital sector for econ omic revitalisation of Jammu & 
Kashmir and sustained focus on diversification, inf rastructure strengthening and 
confidence-building measures will be essential to maintain the growth momentum. 
 
(Para 5.8.29) 
MIGRANT REHABILITATION 
 The Committee notes that 47,466 migrant families co ntinue to be registered for 
relief and that substantial financial and welfare a ssistance is being provided. The 
Committee appreciates the completion and allotment of 5,248 two-room tenements in 
Jammu and the progress made in construction of tran sit accommodations in the Valley. 
However, the Committee observes that while 4,112 tr ansit accommodations have been 
completed, 1,888 units remain under construction. T he Committee recommends that the 
remaining units be completed in a time-bound manner to ensure secure accommodation for 
employees appointed under the special package. 
(Para 5.8.33) 
 The Committee notes that 5,896 out of 6,000 sancti oned posts have been filled. 
While this represents significant progress, the Com mittee recommends that the remaining 
vacancies be filled expeditiously so that the emplo yment component of the rehabilitation 
package is fully realised. 
(Para 5.8.34) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the implementation of Di rect Benefit Transfer (DBT) 
mechanisms, digitisation of documentation processes  and issuance of Pradhan Mantri Jan 
Arogya Yojana PM-JAY SEHAT cards, which enhance tra nsparency and access to 
services.  
 
(Para 5.8.35) 
 
 The Committee recommends that financial relief, th ough necessary may 
progressively be complemented by long-term liveliho od generation, entrepreneurship 
promotion and integration measures. Although, migra nt rehabilitation is not merely a 
welfare measure but also a sensitive socio-economic  and humanitarian issue and sustained 
efforts, adequate housing, secure employment, commu nity confidence-building and 
infrastructure support in areas of return are essen tial for ensuring dignified and 
sustainable reintegration. 

173 
 
(Para 5.8.36) 
 
DEMAND NO. 59 - TRANSFERS TO PUDUCHERRY 
 
 The Committee notes that Central Assistance contin ues to constitute a significant 
component of the resource structure of the Union Te rritory. While the allocation for     
2026-27 maintains parity with RE 2025-26, there exists a substantial gap between projected 
demand and allocated resources, particularly in res pect of infrastructure and externally 
aided projects.  
(Para 5.9.6) 
  The Committee recommends that the Ministry may re view the 
resource position during the course of the financia l year and consider additional support at 
the Revised Estimates stage, particularly for infra structure and externally aided projects, 
based on progress of implementation. Continued effo rts may be made to strengthen own 
revenue mobilisation, rationalise expenditure and i mprove fiscal sustainability so that the 
Union Territory may gradually reduce its long-term dependence on Central Assistance and 
borrowings.   
(Para 5.9.7)

CHAPTER – I 
OVERVIEW 
1.1 Introduction 
 
1.1.1 The North Eastern Region (NER) of India, comprising the eight States of Arunachal 
Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura, represents 
nearly eight per cent of the country’s geographical area and is home to approximately 4.5 crore 
people. Characterized by rich biodiversity, abundant forest resources, heavy precipitation and 
diverse cultural heritage, the region holds immense potential for sustainable and inclusive 
development. The NER shares international borders with Nepal, Bhutan, China, Myanmar and 
Bangladesh, giving it strategic importance in India’s Act East policy. As per the India State of 
Forest Report 2021, the North Eastern States account for nearly 23.75 per cent of the country’s 
total forest cover. With over 81 per cent of its population residing in rural areas, the region’s 
development priorities remain closely linked with infrastructure creation, livelihood generation, 
connectivity enhancement and improvement in social services. 
 
1.1.2 The Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER) was constituted 
initially as a Department in 2001 and later upgraded to a full-fledged Ministry in 2004. It was 
established with the primary objective of ensuring focused attention on the unique 
developmental needs of the North Eastern States and fostering effective coordination between 
State Governments of North Eastern State and various Central Ministries/Departments. 
Ministry of DoNER is the only Ministry of the Government of India with a territorial 
jurisdiction, entrusted with the responsibility of coordinating and monitoring developmental 
efforts across the NER. 
 
1.1.3 The Ministry of DoNER aims to transform North Eastern Region through development, 
in sustainable yet accelerated manner, affording comprehensive growth and access to ease of 
living to all its citizens. The following are the main objectives of the Ministry: 
 
(i) Synergize policies, plans and execution for rapid development of NERegion through 
Collaborating with Central Ministries, States, Agencies & Expert Stakeholders; 
 
(ii) Ensuring full utilization of 10% Gross Budget Support (GBS) and other budgetary 
resources for NER; 
 
(iii) Promoting investment in the NER, including public, private, corporate & multilateral 
funding; 
 
(iv) Developing infrastructure to mitigate connectivity and social sector deficits of the 
region, and Strengthening institutions and networks for livelihood, social services, 
skills and capacity. 
 
1.1.4 To realize these objectives, the Ministry implements various Schemes for development 
of North East Region viz. North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (Roads)-
NESIDS (Roads), North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme Other Than Road-
NESIDS(OTRI), Schemes of North Eastern Council (NEC), PM-DevINE scheme alongwith 
Special Development packages (SDPs) for Assam and Tripura.  In addition to the Ministry 
also coordinates with other stakeholders, who can be from non-government sector or 
multilateral sector, to work for the development of NER. 
 

2 
 
1.2 Mandates and Responsibilities of the Ministry of DoNER 
 
1.2.1  The Ministry of DoNER is mandated to: 
(i) Plan, execute and monitor development schemes and projects in key sectors such as 
power, irrigation, roads and communications. 
 
(ii) Implement flagship schemes including the North East Special Infrastructure 
Development Scheme (NESIDS), the Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources 
(NLCPR), and other infrastructure and livelihood initiatives. 
 
(iii) Oversee and coordinate with institutions under its administrative control such as the 
North Eastern Council (NEC), North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing 
Corporation Limited (NERAMAC), North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms 
Development Corporation Limited (NEHHDC), North East Development Finance 
Corporation Ltd (NEDFi), and the North East Cane and Bamboo Development 
Council (NECBDC). 
 
(iv) Promote livelihood and community-based programmes including the North Eastern 
Region Community Resource Management Project (NERCORMP). 
 
1.3 Demand No. 23 of the Union Budget 2025–26 pertains to the Ministry of 
Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER).  
 
1.3.1  The Demand provides for the administrative expenditure of the Ministry and its 
attached offices, grants-in-aid to State Governments and institutions, capital outlay for 
infrastructure development, and financial assistance under various Central Sector Schemes 
aimed at the socio-economic development of the North Eastern Region (NER). 
 
The allocations under Demand No. 23 are structured to ensure: 
(i) Effective implementation of flagship development schemes; 
(ii) Strengthening of institutional mechanisms in the NER; 
(iii) Bridging critical infrastructure gaps; 
(iv) Promotion of entrepreneurship, livelihood and skill development; and 
(v) Enhanced coordination and monitoring of projects in the region. 
1.3.2   Major Heads of Expenditure under Demand No. 23 
The Demand comprises provisions under the following broad categories: 
(i)  Secretariat – General Services: This head provides for salaries, and 
administrative expenses of the Ministry. 
 
(ii)  Other Administrative Services – North Eastern Council, Shillong: Other 
Administrative Services, relating to Salaries and other administrative expenses of the 
North Eastern Council, Shillong; 
 

3 
 
(iii)  North Eastern Areas –This component includes allocations for 
implementation of major development schemes in the region, namely: 
 
a. Schemes of the North Eastern Council (NEC); 
b. North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS); 
c. Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE); 
d. Technical Assistance for ‘Enhancing Landscape & Ecosystem 
Management(ELEMENT);and  
e. Special Development Packages. 
 
1.3.3   These allocations are primarily directed towards infrastructure creation, connectivity 
improvement, social sector interventions, and institutional strengthening. 
(iv)   (Capital Outlay on Miscellaneous General Services – North Eastern Council) 
Other Administrative Services, relating to Machinery and Equipment, Information, 
Computer, Telecommunication (ICT) Equipment and other Capital Miscellaneous 
Expenditure of the North Eastern Council, Shillong. 
 
(v)   (Capital Outlay on Miscellaneous Secretariat General Services) 
 Secretariat General Services, covering the Information, Computer, Telecommunication 
(ICT) Equipment and other Capital Miscellaneous Expenditure of the Ministry;  
 
(vi)   (Capital Outlay on North Eastern Areas) 
 
a.  Schemes of North Eastern Council [Capital outlay]; 
b.  North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS); 
c.  Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE); 
d.  North East Road Sector Development Scheme – Programme Component; and 
e.  Schemes under the Social and Infrastructure Development Fund (SIDF). 
 
(vii)  Other Loans to Industries & Minerals - Financial assistance is provided under the 
North East Entrepreneurs Development Scheme (NEEDS) through North East Development 
Finance Corporation Ltd (NEDFi) to catalyze entrepreneurship and industrial growth in the 
North Eastern States. 
1.4  Coordination with Central Ministries and Departments 
1.4.1 The Ministry plays a critical coordinating role in ensuring effective implementation of 
development schemes in the NER. It monitors expenditure under the mandatory 10 percent 
GBS earmarked for the region by non-exempted Central Ministries and Departments. Regular 
sectoral review meetings are held with key Ministries such as Railways, Road Transport & 
Highways, Civil Aviation, Power, Environment, and Tourism to ensure timely completion of 
projects. 
1.4.2 The Ministry also participates in Inter-Ministerial Groups and is consulted during 
policy formulation and appraisal processes through EFC/SFC and Cabinet notes. Five Inter-
Ministerial Committees (IMCs) focus on Roads, Health & Nutrition, Medicinal & Aromatic 
Plants, HADP, and Science & Technology interventions in NER (STINER). 
 

4 
 
1.5  Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) for NER 
1.5.1 According to this extant policy of the Government, all non-exempted Central 
Ministries/ Departments are mandated to spend at least 10% of their GBS of Central Sector 
and Centrally Sponsored Schemes for NER.  This is aimed at ensuring a quantum jump in 
budgetary resource-flow to the region in order to address the existing backlog and gaps in 
minimum basic services and infrastructure. 
1.5.2   MDoNER, being the nodal Ministry, monitors and keeps track of expenditure under 
mandatory 10% GBS by non-exempted Ministries/Departments through a meticulous system of 
expenditure tracking. This exercise is being undertaken on quarterly basis and the allocation & 
actual expenditure figures by respective Ministries/Departments are collected, compiled and 
forwarded annually to Ministry of Finance for vetting. 
1.5.3  The Ministry-wise details of expenditure (provisional) Quarter-wise up to 30.09.2025 for 
FY 2025-2026 are given at Annexure.  
1.6 Institutions under the Ministry of DoNER 
1.6.1  North Eastern Council (NEC) 
1.6.2 The North Eastern Council (NEC) was constituted as a statutory advisory body by an 
Act of Parliament under the NEC Act, 1971 (84 of 1971) marking the beginning of a new 
chapter of concerted and planned endeavor for rapid socio-economic development of the North 
Easter Region (NER). NEC is looking to continue its efforts, especially in terms of gap-filling 
in areas which have escaped the attention of various development agencies, and creating 
convergence at different levels. NEC is also looking at building capacities, sharing best 
practices and introducing cutting edge technologies among the NE states. 
1.6.3 Major Achievements/Activities of NEC during the Year 2025 
(i) During January to December, 2025, under Schemes of NEC, a total of 33 projects worth 
₹252.97 Crores were sanctioned and 100 projects worth ₹482.86 Crores were completed 
 
(ii) During the same period, sixteen (16) projects worth ₹ 607.75 Cr. were sanctioned, sixteen 
(16) projects worth ₹580.29 Cr. were completed under NESIDS-Roads.  
 
(iii) Seven major projects (₹10.00 Cr. and above) worth ₹131.88 Crores completed under 
Schemes of NEC during this period. 
 
1.7  North East Cane and Bamboo Development Council (NECBDC) 
1.7.1 North East Cane and Bamboo Development Council (NECBDC) [erstwhile Cane and 
Bamboo Technology Centre (CBTC)] is an ISO 9001:2008 certified organization and was 
established in the year 2000 as part of Cane and Bamboo Technological Up-gradation and 
Networking Project of United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). NECBDC was 
registered as a Society on 21st July 2004.NECBDC has been steadfast in its commitment to 
developing the bamboo and cane sector, particularly for the NER.  
 
Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) under administrative control of Ministry of 
DoNER 

5 
 
 
1.8 North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited 
(NERAMAC) 
1.8.1 NERAMAC, incorporated in 1982 as a Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE), 
functions not only as a marketing agency for farmers and entrepreneurs but also undertakes 
diverse initiatives such as Agri-Horti projects, skill curriculum development, input supply, 
promotion of GI produce, organization of agricultural events, and assistance in establishing 
horticulture value chains including food processing, thereby adopting a holistic approach to 
Agri-Horti development.  
 
1.9 North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited 
(NEHHDC) 
1.9.1 (NEHHDC) has been playing a pivotal role in the development, promotion, and 
commercialization of the rich and diverse handicrafts and handlooms of the North Eastern 
Region (NER). The Corporation serves as a vital institutional link between artisans and 
markets by facilitating skill development, entrepreneurship promotion, market access, 
infrastructure support, and value-chain strengthening, while simultaneously preserving the 
region’s unique cultural heritage. 
 
1.10 Bridging Social and Physical Infrastructure Gaps in NER 
 
1.10.1 The Government has proactively undertaken multiple initiatives to develop new 
infrastructure and enhance existing facilities in the NER. These initiatives encompass efforts 
to bolster air, road, rail, waterways, and telecom connectivity in NER through the 
implementation of ongoing and new schemes/projects by various Central 
Ministries/Departments/Organizations. The MDONER is spearheading the implementation of 
vital schemes such as the North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS)-
Roads, NESIDS (OTRI), NERSDS programme component, and Special Development 
Packages (SDP). 
 
1.10.2  Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE) 
1.10.3 The Union Cabinet approved the PM-DevINE Scheme on 12.10.2022, as a Central 
Sector Scheme with 100% Central funding, with a total outlay of ₹6,600 crores for the 4 year 
period from 2022-23 to 2025-26. PM-DevINE aims at rapid and holistic development of the 
North-East Region by funding infrastructure and social development projects based on felt 
needs of the States. It strives to fill gaps in various sectors and will not be a substitute for 
existing Central and State Schemes. 
 
 
1.10.4 The objectives of PM-DevINE are to: 
 
a. Fund infrastructure convergently in the spirit of PM GatiShakti 
b. Support social development projects based on felt needs of the NER 
c. Enable livelihood activities for youth and women 
d. Fill the development gaps in various sectors

1.11  North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) (Roads) 
1.11.1   NESIDS is a central sector scheme, which aims to support filling up the infrastructure 
gaps in identified sectors of the NER such as drinking water supply, power, road connectivity, 
tourism and social infrastructure in the areas of primary and secondary sectors of education and 
health. The NESIDS scheme was approved during 2017-18 and was implemented till 
31.03.2022. The approval for extension of NESIDS Schemes w.e.f. 01.04.2022 till 31.03.2026 
has been accorded by the Government on 4th January, 2023. 
 
1.11.2   The scheme aims to provide specific gap-funding in construction of roads that are not 
getting covered under any other Ministry/Department of Government like MoRTH, DoRD, 
BRO, etc. but are necessary to (a) provide access to remote locations,(b)to markets and (c) from 
a security point of view.  
1.11.3   Till 31.12.2025, 114 projects worth ₹ 5306.70 crore have been sanctioned out of which 
64 projects worth Rs. 2649.32 crore have been physically completed and 50 projects worth Rs. 
2657.37 crores are ongoing under NESIDS (Roads).

vulnerable communities; strengthen local institutions; promote a more sensitive approach to 
the design and implementation of development interventions; enhance the capabilities of the 
people of the region to manage new technologies; promote and preserve indigenous food and 
culture; and increase participation of women in local institutions and decision-making

1.14 North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi) 
1.14.1 North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd (NEDFi) is a public limited 
company established in the year 1995 under the Companies Act 1956.  It is notified as a 
Public Financial Institution under Section 4A of the said Act and registered as a Non-Banking 
Financial Company (NBFC) with the RBI. The core business of the Corporation comprises 
lending activities and fee-based activities. The lending activities are undertaken through the 
project finance and microfinance schemes. The Corporation provides fee-based advisory & 
consultancy services to the Central and State governments. NEDFi has been playing an 
important role in facilitating setting up of new industrial and service sector projects, 
especially on MSME segment, in the North Eastern States.

2.1.3 The Committee notes that the Ministry of DoNER has received a substantial hike 
in its budgetary allocation, rising by 52% from ₹4479.20 crores in RE 2025–26 to 
₹6812.30 crores in BE 2026–27. However, if it is compared to allocation of ₹5915  crores

may also ensure that the State Governments/implementing agencies optimally utilize the 
allocated funds and timely submit the utilization certificates so that huge reductions in

2.3.5 As per the detailed information provided by the Ministry, the overall expenditure during 
2024-25 was ₹3,447.71 crores against the Revised Estimate of ₹4,006.00 crores, which works 
out to 86.06% utilization. The under-utilization of funds during the year 2024-25 was mainly 
attributed to receipt of lesser-than-anticipated demands from the State 
Governments/Implementing Agencies. In the current financial year 2025-26, an expenditure of ₹ 
3,451.95 crores has been incurred against the Revised Estimate of ₹ 4,479.20 crores, which is 
about 77.07% utilization as on 31st December, 2025.  
 
2.3.6 The Ministry has further informed that variations in utilization are primarily due to 
implementation pace of projects, delayed submission of proposals and utilization certificates by 
the States/Implementing Agencies, and procedural compliance in the release of funds. The 
Ministry is in constant touch with the State Governments and concerned agencies to expedite 
project execution and ensure optimal utilization of allocated funds. 
 
2.3.7 For the current financial year 2025-26, the Ministry apprised the Committee that it is 
making all possible efforts to ensure optimal utilization of the resources allocated at the Revised 
Estimate stage. The Ministry further stated that rigorous monitoring regular review meetings and 
continuous follow-ups with the State Governments and Implementing Agencies are being 
undertaken. 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
2.3.8 The Committee notes that during 2024–25, the Ministry could utilize ₹3,447.71 
crores against the Revised Estimate of ₹4,006.00 crores, achieving 86.06% utilization, with 
under-utilization attributed mainly due to lower-than-anticipated demands from the State 
Governments and Implementing Agencies. The Committee further observes that in the 
current financial year 2025–26, expenditure of ₹3,451.95 crores has been incurred against 
the Revised Estimate of ₹4,479.20 crores, reflecting 77.07% utilization as on 31st 
December, 2025. While the Ministry has expressed confidence in fully utilizing the Revised 
Estimates in respect of the  major schemes such as North East Special Infrastructure 
Development Scheme (NESIDS), Schemes of North Eastern Council and Prime Minister’s 
Development Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE) by the end of the financial 

16 
 
year, the Committee is of the view that the remaining balance funds under these schemes 
could be utilized with proper planning. The Committee recommends that for the upcoming 
financial year, the Ministry should prepare a clear roadmap, in consultation with all the 
stakeholders, with defined physical and financial milestones to ensure time-bound and 
optimal implementation of schemes during 2026–27. 
2.3.9 The Committee observes that factors such as delays in submission of proposals, 
pending utilization certificates, procedural compliances, and slow project implementation 
affect optimal fund utilization. While appreciating the Ministry’s efforts in undertaking 
rigorous monitoring, regular review meetings, and sustained follow-ups with the States 
and Implementing Agencies, the Committee recommends that a more structured and time-
bound coordination mechanism maybe institutionalized to ensure timely submission of 
proposals and utilization certificates, and to minimize the procedural bottlenecks. 
2.3.10 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may strengthen advance 
planning and quarterly expenditure forecasting in consultation with State Governments 
and concerned agencies so that the deviations from projected utilization levels are 
identified and addressed at an early stage. The Committee also urges the Ministry to 
ensure full and effective utilization of the Revised Estimates for 2025–26 and to avoid last-
quarter expenditure compression, thereby promoting efficient, outcome-oriented and 
financially prudent implementation of schemes.

3.1 Schemes of North East Council  
 
3.1.1 The North Eastern Council (NEC) was constituted as a statutory advisory body by an 
Act of Parliament under the NEC Act, 1971 (84 of 1971) marking the beginning of a new 
chapter of concerted and planned endeavor for rapid socio-economic development of the North 
Easter Region (NER). NEC is looking to continue its efforts, especially in terms of gap-filling 
in areas which have escaped the attention of various development agencies, and creating 
convergence at different levels. NEC is also looking at building capacities, sharing best 
practices and introducing cutting edge technologies among the NE states. 
 
3.1.2 A Central Sector scheme named “Schemes of North Eastern Council (NEC)” fully 
funded by the Government of India, was under implementation since 10th Finance Commission 
period and is continued till 31.03.2026 to fill up gaps in overall development of the Region. 
Schemes of NEC continued unaltered with critical gap interventions in multiple sectors for 
speedy and holistic development of NER. The Scheme will cover all the eight states of the 
North Eastern Region.  Detailed guidelines for Schemes of NEC were issued on 21st August 
2023.  
 
3.1.3 The Schemes of the North Eastern Council (SoNEC) are a Central Sector initiative 
under the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER), designed to ensure 
integrated socio-economic development of the eight states of the NER. The Scheme functions 
through three components: State Normative Component (42%), Central Agency Component 
(28%), and Focused Development Component (30%), enabling states to propose priority 
projects, supporting multi-state regional interventions, and addressing backward, tribal, border, 
and remote areas respectively. Projects span critical growth sectors such as agriculture & allied, 
education & HRD, health, power, tourism, industry & MSMEs, infrastructure, science & 
technology, and water management, 
 
3.1.4 North Eastern Region Community Resource Management Society (NERCORMS), a 
society under the North Eastern Council (NEC), plays a pivotal role in strengthening rural 
livelihoods and promoting sustainable development across the eight states of India’s North 
Eastern Region. With a strong emphasis on community-based resource management and 
inclusive growth, NERCORMS implements a diverse portfolio of projects under the schemes of 
NEC, aimed at enhancing income generation, strengthening infrastructure, expanding market 
access, and fostering technological advancement throughout the region.  
 
3.1.5 These interventions represent a holistic and multi-sectoral development strategy. By 
integrating infrastructure development with agriculture and allied sectors, value addition, 
tourism promotion, and digital innovation, NERCORMS fosters sustainable livelihoods, 
strengthens community institutions, and enhances economic resilience across the North Eastern 
Region. This integrated approach ensures that development remains inclusive, participatory, and 
aligned with the region’s long-term socio-economic transformation goals.

strict adherence to prescribed timelines and approved cost estimates. It further

3.2 Central Pool of Resources for North East and Sikkim/North East Special

3.2.1 The North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) is a centrally-
funded initiative launched in 2017-18 and extended until 2026. It has been restructured into 
two components: NESIDS (Roads), managed by the North Eastern Council, and NESIDS 
(OTRI), overseen by the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region. NESIDS (OTRI) 
includes unfinished projects from previous schemes such as NLCPR, NESIDS, and HADP. 
This restructuring aims to streamline infrastructure development, ensuring efficient resource 
utilization and effective project implementation in the North Eastern region, thereby 
promoting holistic development and economic growth. The Non-Lapsable Central Pool of 
Resources (NLCPR) scheme, initiated in 1998 and managed by the Ministry of Development 
of North Eastern Region (DoNER) since 2001, aims to bridge infrastructure gaps in the North 
Eastern Region (NER) of India. The scheme funds projects prioritized by State Governments, 
with a 90:10 cost-sharing ratio between the Central and State Governments. Over the years, 
NLCPR has sanctioned numerous projects across various sectors to enhance the region's 
development. In 2017, the North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS)

funding.

CHAPTER – IV 
 
SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES 
4.1 Agriculture and Allied Sectors 
4.1.1 Agriculture plays a very significant role in the North Eastern Region (NER), the 
region’s economy, livelihood and culture depend heavily on agriculture. A large population in 
the region depends on agriculture for employment. Many agricultural products, vegetable, 
fruits and grains are highly perishable in nature, food processing sectors such as drying, 
freezing, canning and packaging help preserve these products and reduce wastage. The 
Ministry apprised the Committee that as informed by Ministry of Food Processing Industries 
(MoFPI), in order to strengthen and overall development of the food processing sector 
including processing of perishable crops like fruits, vegetables, and spices, Mo FPI has been 
incentivizing setting up/expansion of related infrastructure through its two Central Sector 
Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY) and Production Linked Incentive 
Scheme for Food Processing Industry (PLISFPI) and a Centrally sponsored PM 
Formalization of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PMFME) scheme. These schemes are 
demand driven and implemented across the country including NER. There is also provision 
for earmarking of funds especially for NER, out of total budgetary allocation under PMKSY 
and PMFME schemes. Further, with an aim to encourage wider participation of stakeholders 
from NER, there are special concessions for NER applicants. Following preferential 
provisions have been made in component scheme guidelines of PMKSY- 
i. Net Worth requirement reduced to amount equal to grant sought, in comparison to 1.5 
times for general areas;  
ii. Term Loan requirement reduced to 10% of eligible project cost, in comparison to 20% 
for general areas;  
iii. Equity requirement reduced to 10% of eligible project cost, in comparison to 20% for 
general areas; 
iv. Quantum of grant at enhanced level of 50% of eligible project cost, in comparison to 
35% for general public (Subject to the maximum ceiling under respective sub-
schemes);  
v. Requirement of minimum project cost reduced to Rupees One Crore, in comparison to 
rupees Three Crores in r/o Creation/Expansion of Food Processing and Preservation 
Capacities (CEFPPC) projects [for other schemes, no such criteria is fixed]. 
4.1.2 It was further informed that under the schemes of NEC, a total of five (5) projects 
related to food processing industries in the NER, worth ₹28.86 crores have been sanctioned, 
out of which three (3) projects worth ₹25.99 crores are ongoing and two (2) projects worth 
₹2.87 crores have been completed, as on 31.01.2026. 
4.1.3 The information was sought about the steps that have been taken to improve market

4.1.5 Pursuant to the directives of the 71st NEC Plenary, MDoNER has undertaken special

through a Steering Group constituted under the aegis of MDoNER in June 2025. The 
approved Logistics Roadmap focuses on strengthening the policy and regulatory ecosystem to 
enhance connectivity in NER.

preparation of State Logistics Master Plans. Notifications for preparation of these plans are 
already in place in Arunachal Pradesh, Tripura, and Nagaland, while similar exercises are 
underway in other NE States.
