are processed through the Establishment Officer as Secretary to the ACC. These include board level appointments to
Central Public Sector Undertakings and appointments of Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the
Ministries/Departments. In addition, all appointments by promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also
processed through the Establishment Officer.
Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB)
6.4   The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making recommendations for
appointment to the full-time Board level posts of Chief Executive and functional Directors and part-time Chairman in
the Central Public Undertakings.
Administrative Vigilance
6.5   The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for the maintenance of integrity of the
public services and eradication of corruption and coordinates the activities of various Ministries/Departments in that
area.
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)
6.6   Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central Vigilance Commission. It has jurisdiction and power in
respect of all matters to which the executive power of the Union Government extends. The Commission is also entrusted
with the supervision of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). The Commission enjoys the same measure of
independence and autonomy as the Union Public Service Commission.
Joint Consultative Machinery
6.7   The Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) is three-tier machinery consisting of the National Council, the
Departmental Council and the Regional/Office Council. Service matters pertaining to the interests of the generality of
employees or specific groups of them are dealt with by this machinery.
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)
6.8   In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by Government decisions, the
Government has set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) in 1985, which now deals with all cases relating to
service matters which were previously dealt with by Courts upto and including the High Courts.
Staff Welfare
6.9   The Department of Personnel and Training is intimately involved in several staff welfare and similar activities.
Mention in this connection can be made of the institution of Grih Kalyan Kendra (a society registered under the
Societies Registration Act, 1860), the Kendriya Bhandar (a registered cooperative society set up in 1963) and the
Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board (a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860).
6.10 The Department also supports various programmes, which are provided in various Ministries/Departments, Central
Government Employees Welfare Coordination Committee in Central Government offices located outside Delhi,
Residents’ Welfare Associations/Area Welfare Officers, Benevolent Fund and Departmental Canteens.
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
7.0   The Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare is the nodal agency of the Government of India for
formulation of general policy on pension and other retirement benefits, as also for redressal of grievances on retirement
benefits. The Department was set up in 1985 as a part of Ministry of personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and has
been rendering service for the benefit of pensioners since then. The Department has taken a number of steps over the
years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater convenience and welfare of the pensioners.
7.1   This Department, does not deal directly with pensioners but is the focal point for dealing with issues concerning
pensioners and for issue of instructions and guidelines regarding matters pertaining to pensioners.
7.2   The main responsibilities entrusted to this Department are:
          (i)    Formulation of policies and coordination of matters relating to retirement benefits of Central Govt.
employees including Defence and Railways;
          (ii)    Administration of
                 (a)   Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972;
                 (b)   Central Civil Services (Commutation of Pension) Rules, 1981;
                 (c)   Central Civil Services (Extraordinary Pensions) Rules;
                 (d)   General Provident Fund (Civil Services) Rules, 1960;
                 (e)   Deposit Linked Insurance Revised Scheme; and

DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
8.0   The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of the Government of India
for administrative reforms as well as redressal of public grievances relating to the State in general and grievances
pertaining to Central Government agencies in particular. The Department disseminates information on important
activities of the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal through Management
Publications and Documentation. This Department also acts as the nodal agency in regard to Organisation an Methods
activities and offers advice to the Ministries/Departments. It also undertakes activities in the field of international co-
operation and exchanges to promote public service reforms.
8.1   This Department, has, in the last few years, taken several initiatives with a view to bring about improvement in the
functioning and effectiveness of Government Departments. To mention a few, the following are important ones:
          (i)    drawing up an agenda for reforms to be carried out in the Central Government as well as in States; and
          (ii)    undertaking through a Commission, a review of administrative laws which have become obsolete and no
longer need to be in the statute book.
8.2   The Department also initiated an exercise on the part of Departments having public interface to draw up their
individual Citizen’s charter to indicate the commitments of that organization for quality and the time-frame in which
services performed by that organization would be completed for members of the public.

13.1 Justifying the decrease under the minor head ‘Grant-in-aid’, the Ministry informed the Committee that the
provisions under this head of account are used for providing grants-in-aid to the Indian Institute of Public
Administration (IIPA), New Delhi. A decision has been taken to progressively reduce the grant-in-aid by 10% per year,
from the year 2002-2003 onwards for a period of five years, so as to reduce the Government grant by 50%. This has
been done with a view to reduce the dependence of IIPA on Government grants and has been necessitated by the
reduced availability of funds. The decrease under this head is on account of the 10% reduction in the grant-in-aid
compared to the previous year.
13.2 The Committee notes the decision of the Government to make the Indian Institute of Public Administration
(IIPA) financially independent by gradually reducing its dependence on Government for funds. It also opines
that the Government should identify other institutions getting grants-in-aid and help those to gradually become
financially independent. However, the reduction of the grants-in-aid should not be dictated by the criterion of
non-availability of funds, rather by the capability of the institution in maintaining its financial requirements
independently.
14.0 To the query on what prompted the Ministry for making a sharp increase in the allocation under the minor head
“10.01.20” – ‘Other Administrative Expenses’ to the tune of Rs. 5.5 crore, the Ministry stated that the provision under
this minor head is used for implementing a UNDP assisted project called “Strengthening of the State Administrative
Training Institutes (ATIs)”. Provisions had to be made to enable a channelisation of the UNDP grant through the
budget. During 2002-2003, the Planning Commission had not taken the requirements of the UNDP assisted projects into
account in making the final outlay for the Ministry and had therefore made a provision of Rs. 1.33 crore out of the Rs. 9
crore requirement outlay projection of the Ministry to enable continuation of the project. The fixed term of the UNDP
project is done to end in December 2003. Consequently, an allocation of Rs. 5.5 crore has been sought to meet the cost
of the remaining work programme to be taken up during the year.
14.1 The Committee takes note of the need to strengthen State Administrative Training Institutes (ATIs) and
therefore recommends the proposed allocation of the Ministry.
15.   With regard to the provision under minor head “10.02.20” – ‘Other Administrative Expenses’ which has been
stepped up to the tune of Rs.4 crore, which is nearly four times the previous years’ allocation to be used for channelising
UNDP grants in respect of a project for establishing a Center for Public Policy (CPP) at IIM, Bangalore. The Ministry,
in justification of the same has furnished details of specific activities that would be taken up under this project alongwith

DEMAND NO.-74 (UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION)
21.0 The Union Public Service Commission is a constitutional body, created under Article 315 of the Constitution. The
Commission’s charter of duties is given in Article 320  and 321 of the Constitution. In brief, it is the duty of the
Commission to conduct examinations for appointment to services of the Union and to advise Government on all matter
relating to framing of recruitment rules, method of recruitment and the principle to be followed in making promotions
and transfers from one service to another. The Commission is also required to be consulted in respect of disciplinary
matters affecting a civil servant including appeals and memoranda filed by individual Government servants. The
Commission’s advice is also sought regarding any claim for reimbursement of legal proceedings instituted against him
for acts done in execution of his duties and on the question of award of pension for injury sustained by a Government
servant in a civil capacity. By virtue of the provisions made in the relevant Acts, the Commission is required to be
consulted in respect of appointments to certain categories of posts under the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, the
Employees’ State Insurance Corporation and the Employees’ Provident Fund Organization.

CHAPTER – III
POLICY, PROGRAMME AND SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
LAL BAHADUR SHASTRI NATIONAL ACADEMY OF ADMINISTRATION
22.0 The Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) located at Mussoori in Uttaranchal is
primarily an institution for training of entrants to Government service through the annual Civil Service Examination
conducted by the UPSC. The responsibility is discharged by the Academy by means of a Foundational Course
conducted for the bulk of the different services covered by the Civil Services Examination, besides imparting intensive
and in-depth training to entrants to the Indian Administrative Service. The Academy also conducts programmes for in-
service training of IAS officers, including officers appointed to the IAS from State Civil Services. For other services
like the Indian Police Service (IPS), the Indian Revenue Service as well as the different Railway Services, the training

99th report of Committee on HOME AFFAIRS

institutions are the National Police Academy at Hyderabad, the National Academy for Direct Taxes at Nagpur and the
Railway Staff College at Vadodara.
22.1 In so far as the Foundational Course for the All India and the Central Services is concerned, the objectives of this
course is given below:
           (a)    to promote esprit de corps among the probationers of different services, emphasizing the inter-dependence
of various services as part of the higher civil services;
           (b)   to motivate probationers towards developing certain basic professional, administrative and human values;
and
           (c)    to impart a basic understading of the constitutional, political, social, economic, legal, historical, cultural and
administrative framework within which the services function.
22.2 In addition to the induction and professional courses exclusively for IAS officers, the Academy also runs a large
number of short duration courses, from 2-3 days to two weeks period.
22.3 On being asked as to the number of short duration courses conducted by the Academy during the last three years,
the Government informed that in 2000, 19 courses were conducted where 542 participated, 17 courses in 2001 with 350
participation and 8 courses in 2002 with 172 participation. From a perusal of the details of cadre/service for whom it
was intended, it has been observed that out of the 44 courses 3 catered to services other than IAS and 20 courses catered
exclusively to the IAS while no mention was made with regard to 21 courses.
23.   The Committee taking note of the contribution made by the Lal Bahadur National Academy of Administration in
catering to the training needs of services other than the IAS, desires that the Academy should devise short-term in-house
departmental capsule courses for the new entrant officers in respective departments on a quarterly basis. Attending these
courses for all newly posted officers from the level of Under Secretary and above should be made mandatory. Similar
quarterly capsule courses should be devised for new entrants below rank of Under Secretary to impart complete
knowledge about the Department. The course content of the LBSNAA for the junior civil servants should include
subjects like agriculture. By incorporating the detailed knowledge of various departments to the departmental training
programmes, the LBSNAA could increase the time in the inputs for improving the agricultural contents in the
probationers course.
24.   The Committee has also been informed that due to non-clearance of sponsoring authority or for other reasons, the
number of participants actually attending the programme is less than the number of participants who have confirmed
their participation in the course. Besides, there is a sense of declining seriousness on part of the participants, perhaps
because their performance in the training programmes do not count for their promotion or find entry in the Annual
Confidential Reports (ACRs).
25.   The Committee taking note of the declining seriousness of the participants in the training programmes, feel that
this decline is perhaps more due to the lack of relevance to the actual job and as such the course contents should be
made relevant to his/her posting. Further, the training programmes for junior level officers should include components
on self-awareness and human values and inputs that would enable them to improve their basic attitude and have a better
understanding of ground level conditions. The Committee opines that such training programme should include
awareness of the Freedom of Information Act, 2002 for bringing in transparency in the administrative function of the
Government.
26.0 To a question with regard to the objectives and concerns of the training activities of the Academy, the Committee
has been informed that in addition to the objectives of imparting knowledge, developing skills and enhancing policy
formulation capabilities, the Academy also lays stress on bringing about right attitudinal orientation.
26.1 The Committee wanted to know whether training programme on ethics and values are conducted by the Academy.
The Government informed that the Academy conducts two courses of one-week duration each, every year on the theme
“Ethical values in Today’s Administration”. So far, the Academy has conducted seven such courses. The basic issues
dealt with the regarding ethical dilemmas in the Government. The Academy shares the concern that there is an erosion
of the humane aspects of administration. The Academy exposes the trainees to persons of eminence who can serve as
positive role models. Modules on “Self Awareness” and other training inputs like Team Building, Responsive
Administration and Sensitisation to the problems and needs of the people, especially those who belong to the poorer and
backward sections of the society, and Village visit are also conducted aimed at bringing about right attitudinal
orientation in the officer trainees.
26.2 The Ministry further stated that the objective of the programme is to expose the participants to the basic principles

99th report of Committee on HOME AFFAIRS
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/99threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:58:50]
of Ethics/Moral Philosophy; tease them into thinking about the values that underpin the framing and implementation of
public policy; and expose them to the ethical frameworks that policy makers use to resolve sticky public policy issues.
The aim is to create an atmosphere in which participatory learning takes place. A churning of the considerable
experience and knowledge of the participants through sharing and debate is encouraged not only to achieve the stated
objectives of the course but also to bring about a vertical integration of the group.
27.0 While appreciating the efforts of the Academy to imbibe ethics and positive values in the participants, the
Committee recommends that such training should be broad based to cater to maximum number of officers. It is of the
opinion that training programmes need to impart skills for interaction with the public in a humane manner.
27.1 The Committee feels that one of the major reasons for lack of interest especially in the foundation and probationary
courses, is the complacency the trainees have developed that all of them will inevitably be declared as passed. Trainees
who fail in various subjects are allowed to reappear at the next examination and the next and so on till eventually they
are declared as pass. The confirmation of services of those who fail in various subjects makes a mockery of the word
“probationer”. There is urgent need for Government to review their policy regarding probationers who fail in subjects
prescribed in the course. The Committee is of the view that probationers who fails to clear all the examinations set out
for them should be declared as failed and then services terminated. Only in proven cases where a probationer fails for
reasons beyond his control should he be permitted to appear just once more and if he fails again termination of his
service should be the rule.
PUBLIC ENTERPRISES SELECTION BOARD
28.0 Public Sector Enterprises (PSE) under the control of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
play a vital role in the development of the national economy. In order to evolve a sound managerial personnel policy for
the Public Sector Enterprises and, in particular, to advise Government on appointments to the top management posts, the
Government of India constituted a Public Enterprises Section Board (PESB) by a Resolution dated 30 August 1974.
Consequent upon the shift of the secretariat of the PESB from the Department of Public Enterprises to the Department
of Personnel and Training from 9 July 1986, a comprehensive review of the policy relating to the functions,
membership, methodology for selection and infrastructure of the PESB was made by Resolution dated 3 March 1987 of
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. Amendments have been made to the Resolution from time to
time, the latest being made on 19 April 2000.
28.1 The PESB functions as a professional body with a large measure of autonomy. Its function are:
          (i)    to be responsible for the selection and placement of personnel in the posts of Chairman, Managing Director
or Chairman-cum-Managing Director (Level I), and Functional Director (Level II) in PSEs as well as in posts
at any other level as may be specified by the Government;
          (ii)   to advise the Government on matters relating to appointment, confirmation or extension of tenure an
termination of the services of personnel of the above mentioned levels;
          (iii)   to advise the Government on the desired structure at the Board level, and for senior management personnel,
for each PSE or group of PSEs;
          (iv)  to advise the Government on a suitable performance appraisal system for both the PSEs and the managerial
personnel in such enterprises;
          (v)   to build a data bank containing data relating to the performance of PSEs and its officers;
          (vi)  to advise the Government on formulation and enforcement of a Code of Conduct and Ethics for managerial
personnel in PSEs; and
          (vii) to advise the Government on evolving suitable training and development programmes for management
personnel in PSEs.
28.2   The PESB consists of one part-time or full-time Chairperson and three full-time Members. The Chairperson and
Members shall be persons who have had a long and distinguished career in management of public or private
corporations or public administration and have a proven record of achievements, preferably, in the field of personnel,
finance, production or marketing. The three full time members of the PESB shall be:

MODERNISATION OF GOVERNMENT OFFICES
30.   The Committee has been informed that modernization of any office must result in betterment of working
environment, increase in efficiency and should facilitate better flow of record and better delivery of services to the
public. Some of the othe attributes of modernized offices are as follows:---
          (a)   Optimal utilization of space by having a good functional lay out with modular furniture where files and
documents of current use are accessed easily.
          (b)   Storage facilities that have the appropriate size and shape which accommodate books/ledgers in the
Ministries/Departments.
          (c)   Provision of proper seating space for members of the public in public dealing sections and also free up staff
time by better record management so that the staff is able to look after public needs better.
          (d)   Proper seating arrangement to facilitate supervision.
          (e)   Providing suitable electric points to facilitate computerization.
31.0 The Committee is of the view that modernizing the entire administrative apparatus should not be an end in itself.
There should be an attitudinal change in the civil servants to serve the public at large. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Government should work out ways to imbibe attitudinal change in its personnel for better delivery
of services to the public.
31.1 The Committee also urges upon the Government to evolve clearly measurable parameters to assess the degree of
improvement made and also monitor those parameters on an effectively periodic basis.
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF SMART GOVERNMENT
32.0 SMART is acronym for Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive and Transparent. The Ministry has initiated
several measures towards achieving the goal of operationalising SMART administration. The conference of Chief
Minister held in New Delhi on 29 May 1997 represented the culmination of the National Debate on Effective and
Responsive Administration. The Action Plan prepared for the Conference dealt with three themes, namely, making
administration accountable and citizen-friendly, ensuring transparency and Right to Information and taking measures to
cleanse and motivate Civil Services. The following are the major components of the aforesaid action plan, which are
also being operationalised:---
          (i)   Citizen’s Charter;
          (ii)   Information and Facilitation Counters (IFCs);
          (iii)  Redress of Public Grievance;
          (iv)  Review of Laws, Regulations and Procedures;
          (v)  Transparency in Government and Right to Information; and
          (vi)  A minimum Agenda for e-governance.

GOOD GOVERNANCE
34.0 Accountability has become the worst casualty because the officers who are to enforce accountability are being
increasingly marginalized in the choice of appointing their subordinates to various posts, specially in the field which is
the cutting edge vis-a-vis the people. Responsibility and rights are inseparable. There is need to restore the rights of the
executive to enable it to discharge its responsibility regarding making itself accountable.
34.1 To a query posed by the Committee with regard to the specific areas/issues identified, the Government gave the
reply that in order to bring about good governance, the areas/issues identified includes – (i) review of administrative
laws; (ii) formulation of Citizen’s charters by the Central Ministries/Departments as also by State Governments; (iii)
setting up of Information and Facilitation Counters in the Ministries/Departments for easy and hassle free access of
information by the citizen; (iv) strengthening the public Grievance Redress Mechanism which is in place in various
Ministries/Departments of the Central Government; (v) implementation of a minimum agenda for promotion of e-
governance for re-engineering of various processess with a view to ensure quicker delivery of public services; and (vi)
documentation and dissemination of best practices in the area of administrative reforms.
35.   The Committee is of the view that with the help of e-governance, computers, improvement of information
technology, Freedom of Information and Citizen’s Charters, collection of basic data and information available with the
Ministry will show a marked improvement if they are constantly updated. The Committee hopes that not only statistical
information but the parameters of decision making also should in due course be made available to the people.

41.0 The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances coordinates the efforts to formulate and
operationalise citizen’s/user’s charter by the Central Government Ministries/Departments and their
PSUs/autonomous/statutory bodies in areas in which they provide services to the members of the public. The
Department also coordinates the efforts of formulating and operationalising Citizen’s Charter in various States/UTs.
41.1 The Committee has been informed that 19 Ministries/Departments have brought out 79 Citizen’s Charters.
Similarly, 23 organizations of the State Governments/UT Administrations have brought out 498 Citizen’s   Charters. 4
Regional Seminars on Citizen’s Charter were organized in 2001-2002 at Hyderabad, Mussoorie, Bhopal and Guwahati

media etc. on the same platform to share experiences in formulation and implementation of Citizen’s Charters. In all 24
State Governments/UT Administrations and 15 Central Government Ministries/Departments/Organizations participated

42.   While taking note of the number of Citizen’s Charters brought out by Central Government Ministries/Departments

Ministries/Department and States/UTs who have not brought out their Citizen’s Charters. Copies of Citizen’s Charters

INFORMATION & FACILITATION COUNTERS
43.0 Information and Facilitation Counter (IFC) is the visible face/physical manifestation of Citizen’s Charter
formulated by an organization. IFCs are setup outside the security zone of each office with a view to facilitating the
dissemination of the information to the citizen/user at one place without the hassle of getting an entry pass. Information
is disseminated through printouts, brochures, book-lets, display boards and sometimes telephonically too.
43.1 Computerised Information and Facilitation Counters have been set up in various
Ministries/Departments/Organisations, etc. of the Government of India to provide information and assistance to the

45.3 The grievances received in this department are sent to the concerned Ministries/Departments and other
organisations of Government for redress under intimation to the petitioner. The Department of AR&PG, however, takes

45.4 Regular meetings are held by AS (AR&PG) with Directors of Grievances of Ministries/Departments/ Organisations

46.   The Committee feels that there is need for publicity (India wide) through Doordarshan to enable the rural folk to
know about the existence of these two channels for the redressal of public grievances. Secondly in some cases the
replies received by the aggrieved do not provide solace and redressal expected from the grievance redressal mechanism
of the Government. The output, it is felt cannot reach the desired level without putting an effective Department-wise
monitoring mechanism that studies the measurable parameters which show tangible results.
47.
   Among various other measures taken by the Government to strengthen the grievance redress mechanism, a uniform
software called Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System has been installed in 22 Ministries/Departments and
13 other organizations. The internet version of this system was launched on 31.05.2002 
(http://DARPG.grievance/nic.in). A citizen can launch his/her grievance on this website and can also monitor the action

to Government agencies with large public interface has also been introduced.
48.   The Committee, while taking note of the above measures to strengthen the grievance mechanism, recommends that
all out efforts should be made to effectively monitor the same and due attention should be given to timely redressal of
grievances lodged. It is also of the considered view that officers responsible for brooking delay should be made
accountable and suitable action taken against them. This mechanism may bring some success to computer savvy public,
but the bulk of India lives in villages. It is therefore that stress has been laid for evolving a mechanism that would serve
the less literates. The Committee expresses a desire to see the results of one such monitoring of each Department.

51.0 Pursuant to the provision of Article 323A of the Indian Constitution, the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 was
enacted by Parliament to set up Administrative Tribunal for adjudication of disputes and complaints with regard to
recruitment and condition of services of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of
the Union and the States.
51.1 Administrative adjudication, which is quasi-judicial in nature, is the main function of Administrative Tribunals.
The basic objective of enacting the Administrative Tribunal Act was:
          (i)    to relieve congestion in the ordinary set of courts; and
          (ii)    to provide for speedy disposal of disputes relating to service matters.
51.2 The Central Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 provides that the Tribunal shall not be bound by the procedure laid
down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 but shall be guided by the principle of natural justice and subject to the other
provisions of Administrative Tribunals Act and rules made by the Central Government. The Tribunal shall have power
to regulate its own procedure including the fixing of places and times of enquiry. As a result of the judgement of the
Supreme Court in the case of L. Chandra Kumar dated 18 March 1997, the appeals against the orders of an
Administrative Tribunals lie before the Division Bench of the concerned High Court.
51.3 Administrative Tribunals are distinguishable from the ordinary Courts with regard to their jurisdiction and
procedure. They are free from the shackles of many of the technicalities of the ordinary Courts. The litigant(s) has to
submit an application in paper book form prescribed by rule 4 of Central Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules,
1985. It means that every application should be accompanied by a proper containing the following:-
          (i)    Certified copy of the order against which the application has been filed;
          (ii)    All documents relied upon by the applicants and mentioned in the application;
          (iii)   Details of the crossed Demand Draft or crossed Indian Postal Order representing the application fee of Rs.
50/-; and
          (iv)   Index of documents.
        The aggrieved person can appear before the Court personally. Government can also present its case through its
Departmental officers or legal practitioners.
51.4 The Tribunal consists of a sanctioned strength of one Chairman, 16 Vice-Chairmen and 49 Members. The
Members are drawn from both judicial as well as administrative streams so to give the Tribunal the benefit of expertise
both in legal and administrative spheres.
51.5 The Committee, in its 87th Report on Demands for Grants (2002-2003) of the Ministry had recommended that the
process of selection of persons to fill up vacancies in the CAT should be initiated at least three months before its
occurrence to avoid a vacuum in the Tribunals. The Government had in its reply stated that the selection processes are
conducted in advance. However, due to litigation of some other unavoidable norms, the selection process is held up.
51.6 To a query regarding the present position of vacancies in the CAT, the Government informed that 4 posts of Vice-
Chairman and 10 posts of Administrative members are laying vacant in various Benches of CAT.
51.7 A perusal of the reasons/present status of vacancy assigned to by the Government shows that in the case of 5
Administrative Members in Allahabad, Guwahati, Ernakulam, Patna and Mumbai Benches, the date on which the
vacancy occurred had been stated ranging from 22.1.2003 to 1.3.2003 and the vacancy circular issued on 31.1.2003 with
last date of receipt of candidatures on 10.3.2003. It has also been further stated that meeting of the Selection Committee
will be organized after obtaining convenience of its members.

59.0 The Central Vigilance Commission is an apex body exercising general superintendence and control over vigilance
matters in administration of Ministries/Departments/Organisations of Central Government was conceptualized under
Government of India Resolution dated 11 February 1964. The Commission is headed by the Central Vigilance
Commissioner who is assisted by a Secretary who is of the rank of Additional Secretary to the Government of India, two
additional Secretaries of the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India and other supporting officers and staff.
There are thirteen Commissioners of Departmental Inquiries (CDI) who conduct oral inquiries relating to major penalty
proceedings on behalf of the disciplinary authorities in serious and important disciplinary cases.
59.1 On being asked as to how many cases are pending for implementation of the advice of the CVC in the
Ministries/Department till date, the Ministry submitted the information provided by the CVC, as per which 4466 cases
of first stage and 1544 cases of second stage advice given by the CVC are pending with various
Ministries/Departments/Organisations. As per the information as contained in the CVC Annual Report the number of
cases pending for more than six months in which the CVC has not received information about implementation of its
advice from various disciplinary authorities are indicated below:-

1997 1975 1202 3177

59.2 The Ministry also stated that some of the factors causing delay in finalisation of proceedings/Departmental action
are:-
          (a)   Duplication in the process of disciplinary proceedings by seeking advance explanation of the officer against
whom the disciplinary enquiry is to be instituted.
          (b)   Allowing of irrelevant documents/witness as in the course of conduct of disciplinary proceedings.
          (c)   Improper listing of documents in charge-sheet thereby giving an opportunity to the Charged Officer to delay
the proceeding.

59.3   In this regard, the Ministry further informed the Committee that the following measures are contemplated for

          (a)   Non-admission of irrelevant documents and proper listing of documents in the charge-sheet has been

          (b)   Rigorous criteria has been adopted in selection of Inquiry Officers.

60.0 The Committee takes serious note of the high pendency of cases for implementation of advice of the CVC in the
Ministries/Departments. In administration the objective of rewards and punishment gets completely defeated unless they
are awarded with utmost promptness. This is specially true about punishments. As promptness in punishments has a
salutary effect on the tone of administration and in the light of the fact that the CVC is directly responsible to the
Parliament, there appears no escape for the Committee but to directly involve itself through an in-depth study of the
problem of delays of more than six months in thousands of cases. The Ministry has enumerated six reasons for the
delays. The Committee therefore would like to have break up of all the delayed cases of the past five years that are
respectively attributable to the six stated reasons in para 59.2. It would further like to know the specific remedial
measures that Government intends to adopt to tackle each of the six categories of reasons respectively. Additionally, the
Committee would like to know how the Government intend to implement each of the measures it so suggests for
example, in the measures already suggested by the Government in Para 59.3; how exactly will it be possible to
implement the measures given at (a) & (b) in Para 59.3. Further, in what way are the delays going to be reduced by
resorting to action proposed in (c), (d) & (e) of Para 59.3 ? Of the measures contemplated to curb delays, barring (a) of
Para 59.3, none of the other measures contemplated seem to have any direct bearing on the ‘causes of delay’ as
enumerated in clauses (a), (c), (d), (e) & (f) of Para 59.2. That being the case, the Committee has grave doubts if the
measures contemplated will at all make any dent on the problem of delays.
60.1 Till an in-depth study is made by the Committee to effectively deal with this problem in a systematic and sustained
basis, the Committee has the following to suggest:
As each case of punishment has its own unique complexities, it is therefore suggested that in the light of the
complexities of each case which would be apparent to the CVC before it tenders the first stage advise, the CVC
must prescribe specific time frames with dates by which Ministries/Departments/Organisations must report to the
CVC about the implementation of CVC’s first stage advice. The same should be done in respect of the second
stage advice. If the Ministries/Departments/Organisations find that the time frame prescribed by the CVC is
impractical, they themselves must inform the CVC within seven days of the receipt of the advice as to the date by
which they shall be able to report the said implementation. If, thus the Ministries/Departments/Organisations fail to
keep up to their own suggested dates, the CVC should report to the head of the Department for taking action
against the dealing officer for inability to abide by his own date. Initially, warnings to such officers should be
placed on their personal files but if his performance does not improve even after three warnings, major punishment
proceedings should be initiated against that officer for incompetent handling of his duties. The Committee believes
that the root of the problem of delays lies in the absence of accountability of the dealing officers of the CVC, and
the dealing officers of the Ministries/Departments/Organisations and it is here where the action should commence
forthwith.
60.2 In the Meanwhile, the Committee, in consultation with the Ministry and the CVC shall in due course evolve a
permanent operational procedure.
SCHEME FOR COMPASSIONATE APPOINTMENT
61.0 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions devises welfare measures for the Central Government
employees. The scheme for compassionate appointment is one of the welfare measures.

99th report of Committee on HOME AFFAIRS
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/99threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:58:50]
61.1 The object of the scheme is to grant appointment on compassionate ground to a member of the dependent family
(spouse, son, daughter, brother or sister) of a Government employee dying in harness or who takes retirement on
medical grounds, thereby leaving his family in penury and without any means of livelihood, to relieve the family of the
Government employee concerned from financial destitution and to help it get over the emergency.
61.2 The Scheme for compassionate appointment has been last revised/simplified and consolidated in the light of
various Court judgements. Fifth Central Pay Commission Report and the Study Reports of 1990 and 1994 prepared by
the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances in October 1998.
61.3 To a questions as to how far the scheme has served the welfare of the Government employees whose near relations
have opted for compassionate appointment, the Ministry has stated that the scheme for compassionate appointment
provides for compassionate appointments in Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ posts to the extent of 5% of the vacancies to be filled by
direct recruitment in Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ posts. It is further stated that the compassionate appointment is to be granted
only in most deserving cases to save the dependent family of a deceased/medically retired Government employees from
financial destitution. The Ministry has stated that the Scheme has its utility as a welfare measure.
62.0 Certain other specific questions had been put to the Ministry Viz.
          (a)   How far has the scheme served the welfare of Government employees ?
          (b)   Whether the implementation of the scheme was ever monitored to assess the extent to which families of
Government employees have been benefited and what are the details of such assessment?
          (c)   Whether the Ministry has ever collected data as to the number of deserving families that could not be helped
under this scheme ?
          (d)   Whether any Court Judgement/Order has defined what is “a family in penury”?
          (e)   Whether any supplementary guidelines defining “indigent conditions” were issued?
          (f)    Did the original scheme envisage the maintaining of a waiting list? What is the period of validity of such
waiting lists?
          (g)   As per the scheme, if the entire 5% vacancies are full in one Ministry/Department, whether appointment on
compassionate grounds could be made in any other Government of India Ministry/Department? Accordingly,
was any waiting list monitored to enable their accommodation in other Departments?
          (h)   How many cases on the waiting list of one Department were accommodated in other Departments during the
preceding 10 years?
          (i)    Whether calculation of 5% vacancies was affected by the ban on fresh recruitments? Has it meant a reduction
or is the 5% being calculated on the basis of the original sanctioned strength?
          (j)    Was there any time bar for compassionate appointments under this scheme?
          (k)   Whether the dependants of the deceased employees were permitted to retain Government accommodation in
anticipation of compassionate appointments?
          (l)    Whether the Ministry deems fit to consider giving a Group ‘D’ post to an applicant of Group ‘C’ post to
reduce the distress of the family?
          (m)  Whether DPOT or the Directorate of Estate prescribes any time limit regarding retention of the Government
Accommodation by family of the deceased employee? If so, what is that time limit?
62.1
 The responses of the Ministry to the afore-mentioned questions are not satisfactory. The committee feels that the
matter of compassionate appointments requires detailed discussion to formulate its
views/suggestions/recommendations. The Committee, therefore, requests the Ministry to furnish clear-cut answers
to the afore-mentioned questions within six weeks time from the date of presentation of its Report of Parliament to
enable it to hold discussion on the subject.

The Central Para Military Forces : 
The different Central Para -military Forces namely. BSF. ITBP . CRPF, Assam Rifles and•CISF 
have been raised for different purpose s. Border Security Force (DSF) is primarily meant for 
border deployment to check infiltration, trans-border crimes on the Indo-Pakistan and Indo · 

19 
Bangladesh border. Indo Tibetan Border Polioe (ITBP) performs similar role on the Indo-Tabet 
border and in J&K , Himachal Pradesh and Utta r Pradesh , Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) 
has been raised to assist States/UTs in interna l security duties. Assam Rifles (A R) is meant for 
providing security of North-Eastern sector and the international border and carry out counter­
insurgency operations in North-Eastern States. Central Indust rial Security Force (ClSF) bas been 
raised for the protection and security of industrial undertakings owned by the Central 
Government. For internal security duties, CRPF is the primary 'force. The current problem of

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One hundredth Report on the Demands for Grants (2003-04) relating to the Department
of Development of North Eastern Region.
2. The Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary of the Department in its sitting held
on 26th March, 2003.
3. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied upon the
following:—
(i) Presentation made by the Secretary of the Department;
(ii) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Department for the year 2003-04;
(iii) Explanatory Notes on the Demands for Grants (2003-04) received from the
Department;
(iv) Annual Report of the Department for the year 2002-03;
(v) Written replies furnished by the Department to the Questionnaire sent to it by the
Secretariat; and
(vi) Written clarifications to the points/issues raised by the Members in the meetings of the
Committee.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on 9th April, 2003.
5. For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
PRANAB MUKHERJEE

1
REPORT
The North Eastern Region comprises of 8 States of Arunchal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur,
Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura and Sikkim. Excluding Sikkim, the region covers an area
of 255,000 sq. kms representing around 7.8 per cent of the total area of the country. It is a
distinct geographical entity connected with the rest of the country through a narrow corridor in
North Bengal thereby standing out as a classic example of cultural and geographical isolation from
the other composite States of India. The region shares 98 per cent of its borders with other South
East Asian countries viz. Bhutan and China in the North, Myanmar in the East and Bangladesh in
the South and West.
1.2 The region has a total population of 38.5 million as per 2001 census which is around 3.75
per cent of the country’s population.
1.3 The North Eastern States are categorised as Special Category States which entitles them to
receive 90% of the Central plan assistance as grants. However funds are not allocated State-wise.
Instead, Project specific assistance is released for sanctioned projects under the Central Pool. The
release of funds to the State Governments depends on their capacity to formulate sound project
proposals, utilize the funds released and the pace of implementation of the projects on the ground.
These funding sources and quantum of funds broadly take care of the requirement for development
programmes of the North Eastern States and are intended to continue till the Region reaches a
certain minimum level in terms of infrastructure development.
2. The Department of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) was constituted in
September, 2001. An extract of the amendments to the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961 containing the work allocation to the Department is as follows:
• Matters related to the planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes
and projects of North Eastern region including those in the sectors of power, irrigation,
roads and communications.
• Hill Areas Development Programme and Border Areas Development Programme in
North Eastern region.
• Non-lapsable fund for the North Eastern region.
• North Eastern Council.
• North Eastern Development Finance Institution (NEDFI).
• North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited (NERAMAC).
• Sikkim Mining Corporation Limited (SMC).
• North Eastern Handlooms and Handicrafts Development Corporation (NEHHDC).
• Road works financed in whole or in part by the Central Government in the North
Eastern region.
• Planning of road and inland waterways transport in the North Eastern region.
3. The thrust of the Department in the development of North Eastern region consists of
improving infrastructure, providing greater access to basic social services like education, health,
drinking water and sanitation, etc., expanding economic and social opportunities for all, building

2
capacities aimed at increased efficiency, creating an environment for private participation conducive
to growth, and providing a policy frame to influence in a positive manner, wide ranging economic
activities having employment/income generation potential.
BUDGET OF DEPARTMENT OF DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH EASTERN REGION

was for 2002-03. However, in 2002-03 the total allocation towards plan expenditure for DoNER
in BE 2002-03 was Rs. 469.90 crores and Non-Plan expenditure Rs. 8.61 crore approximately
while in RE 2002-03 plan expenditure was Rs. 1019.90 crore and Non-Plan expenditure
Rs. 7.53 crore. The Ministry of Finance and Company Affairs has approved Rs. 7.8 crore towards
Non-Plan expenditure during 2003-04. The Planning Commission has approved plan assistance of
Rs. 569.90 crore for DoNER and Rs. 500 crore for the Plan schemes of NEC. The detailed

6.1 The Secretary, DoNER in his deposition before the Committee, stated that DoNER was
one of the few Departments which had fully utilised the Plan allocation for the year 2002-03
despite the fact that the first release was made in September, 2002 and second was in the end of

PLAN SCHEMES OF DoNER
7. The Plan Schemes relating to the Department consist of:-
(i) Other Social Services
* Advocacy and Publicity
* Technical Assistance and Capacity Building
(ii) Industrial Financial Institutions
* Loans to North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd.
(iii) Non-ferrous Mining and Metal Industries
* Equity to Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC)
7.1 Under ‘Other Social Services’, the Department proposes to promote private sector
investment in the region. Accordingly, it organised a Business Summit in Mumbai on
19 and 20 July, 2002. DoNER also proposes to advocate the strengths and potential of the region
through other suitably designed programmes cutting across the Governmental and non-
Governmental sector. It also address the institutional capacity constraints of the region through
Capacity Building and Technical Assistance Programme.
7.2 Under ‘Industrial Financial Institutions’, DoNER extends long term interest free soft loan to
NEDFi. During 2002-03, an amount of Rs.15.40 crore has been disbursed to NEDFi. For
BE 2003-04, a similar amount has been approved.

4
7.3 As part of assistance to non-ferrous mining and metal industry, Sikkim Mining Corporation,
a joint venture of Governments of India and Sikkim with equity share capital ratio of 51:49
respectively, receives funds from the Central Government in proportion to its equity share.
8. When asked about the objectives of DoNER, the Government, in its written reply, has stated
that DoNER attempts to promote development of North Eastern region by creating synergies and
convergence of the various programmes of different Departments of Government of India taking
up activities in the North-East. DoNER, however, has no mechanism or mandate to implement the
projects directly by itself. This apart, for meeting the gaps in the infrastructure sector, DoNER
assists the State Governments and Central agencies. DoNER has also been regularly monitoring the
requirement of 10% expenditure by Central Government Ministries/Departments in the North
Eastern region.
9. Regarding cultural activities the Department has stated that it is taking up cultural and sports
activities in a major way. It has partially funded the Sports Complex in Imphal (Khumlanpak) where
the 1999 National Games were held. In Sikkim, Paljor Stadium has been funded from NLCPR.
Another Sports Hall has been sanctioned this year at Mokokchung in Nagaland. In Bodo
Autonomous Council area in Assam, a mini stadium at Chapaguri and apex stadium at Kokrajhar
have also been sanctioned. In the field of culture, the Shankardev Kalakshetra in Guwahati is also
being assisted by the DoNER. Besides, a large number of schools, colleges and universities have
been assisted under NLCPR. In addition, NEC has also extended support for creation of
infrastructural facility for sports. It has assisted a sports complex each at Aizawal, Silchar and
Agartala. Rs. 34.50 crore has been earmarked for Tenth Plan. The proposed outlay for 2003-04
is Rs. 4 crore. On the cultural side, Fashion Shows, Crafts Exhibition, North Eastern Day and various
other cultural exchange programmes have been sponsored in North Eastern region by the DoNER.
10. On the greater use of Doordarshan for disseminating of information pertaining to the region
the Department has informed that the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has declared the
year 2003 as the “Year of the North East”. On its part, DoNER has also taken up with Prasar
Bharati the need for screening North Eastern news and programmes on the National hookup of
Doordarshan. Besides, strengthening and upgradation of the low power transmitters in the North
Eastern region has been identified as an area to be attended to by the Ministry of Information and
Broadcasting.
11. As regards, ensuring financial discipline in the States of the region, the Department has
stated that in so far as DoNER’s own projects/schemes are concerned, a strict regime of on-
releases based on utilisation, photographs and quarterly progress reports is followed. The States
have been asked to reflect DoNER’s projects in the Annual Budget at the major and minor head
levels so that actual expenditures as per Accountant-General’s accounts can also be verified. For
the general financial discipline among the States, however, DoNER does not have a direct mandate
or authority. DoNER, however, is represented in the Core Group of Officers constituted by
Ministry of Finance which inter alia is looking into these aspects.
12. Regarding funding of more developmental programmes through Central Government
agencies the Department has stated that the budgetary allocation to DoNER is classified as
‘Assistance to State Plan’. Therefore, like State Plan, the DoNER funds are released as 90% Grant
and 10% Loan which is the liability of the respective State Governments. While DoNER does strive
to give as much projects for execution directly by Central Government agencies as it can, this can
only be done if the State Government agrees to it since it is the State Government which would
be repaying the 10% loan. With the consent of the State Governments, the DoNER has engaged
Central Government agencies like Border Roads Organisation (BRO), Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd.
(BHEL), Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL), etc. for execution of some of the
projects.

5
13. In relation to the formulation of a master plan for the region, the Department has stated
that S.P. Shukla Commission Report, 1997, is in the nature of a Master Plan for ‘transforming the
North East’. It has identified the gaps in the infrastructure sector and basic minimum needs in the
North Eastern Region.
14 As for setting up of national institutions like IITs and IIMs in the North Eastern region, the
Department has stated that DoNER is already funding the Central University in Mizoram, North
Eastern Hill University, Shillong, Central University in Nagaland, Central University in Tezpur,
Central University in Silchar, IIT, Guwahati, North Eastern Regional Institute of Science and
Technology (NERIST) in Arunachal, Regional Institute of Medical Sciences at Imphal, etc.
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
15. The North-Eastern Council was set up in 1972, following the enactment of the North
Eastern Council Act, 1971. For a long time, the North Eastern States had been demanding
restructuring of the Council so as to make it more effective. In pursuance of the demand, the
North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Act, 2002 came into force on 23rd December, 2002. In terms
of the amendment, Sikkim has become the eighth member of the Council. The composition of the
Council has been revised and now consists of the Governors and Chief Ministers of Arunachal
Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. In addition, three
members are to be nominated by the President of India to the Council. The President of India may,
if deemed necessary, nominate a Union Minister to be a member of the Council. The Chairman of
the Council will be nominated by the President. By practice, the Governor of one of the
Member States is nominated as Chairman. Presently, the Governor of Assam is the Chairman of
the Council.
15.1 The Council’s functions have also been modified and it is now to function as a regional
planning body for the North-Eastern region. While formulating the regional plan, the Council will
give priority to schemes and projects which benefit two or more States, with the exception of
Sikkim for which the Council will formulate State-specific Projects and Schemes. The Council will
also review, from time to time, implementation of projects and schemes, progress of expenditure
and measures taken by the Member States for the maintenance of security and public order and
recommend to the State Governments further measures to be taken in this regard. For
accomplishing the above functions, the Council shall have such powers as may be delegated to it
by the Central Government. In terms of the amendment, the Council is required to meet at least
twice a year. The amendment also provides for participation of a representative of Department of
Development of North Eastern Region in the meetings of the Council.
NEC Secretariat
15.2. The Secretariat of the North Eastern Council is located at Shillong. The Secretariat is
responsible for the formulation of NEC’s Plan Schemes and their implementation. Secretary heads
the Secretariat. The Secretary is assisted by 12 Sectoral Heads viz. Planning Adviser, Financial
Adviser, Adviser (Transport and Communications), Adviser (Power), Director (Manpower), Ex-
Officio Adviser (Health), Director (S&T), Ex-Officio  Adviser (Forests), Ex-Officio  Adviser
(Minerals), Adviser (Horticulture), Adviser (Banking and Industries) and Adviser (Irrigation and
Flood Control).
15.3 From inception in 1972, NEC Secretariat has been under the administrative control of the
Ministry of Home Affairs. Since September, 2001, the administrative control has been transferred
to DoNER.

TENTH PLAN
17. The Tenth Plan of NEC accords priority to:
(i) Inter-State connectivity by roads to take up the construction of good quality roads
to more conveniently connect different States of the North East.
(ii) Inter-State connectivity by air—to improve air services in the North East by
providing budgetary support to the Indian Airlines/Airports Authority of India and
ensure that existing Airports are upgraded suitably and utilised optimally.
(iii) Augmentation of Power supply by taking up power projects for benefit of more than
one State and extension and improvement of transmission and distribution lines.
(iv) Execution of projects by competent agencies with proper supervision and monitoring.
(v) Promotion of transparency and accountability in implementation of the projects.
(vi) Strengthening of institutions to make them Centres of Excellence.

an outlay of Rs.3500 crore for NEC.

20. The Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) has been constituted out of the
unspent amount from 10% of the budget of various Union Ministries and Departments (except
those specifically exempted) exclusively earmarked for the socio-economic development of the
North East. Budget for the purpose is defined as Gross Budgetary Support to the Plan, which is
inclusive of Externally Aided Projects.
20.1 Until recently, the Planning Commission was handling the Non-lapsable Central Pool of
Resources (NLCPR). The work has since been transferred to DoNER. The broad objective of this
pool is to ensure speedy development of the socio-economic infrastructure in North Eastern region
by increasing the flow of budgetary financing for new infrastructure/projects/schemes in the
region. Both physical and social infrastructure sectors such as irrigation and flood control, power,
roads and bridges, education, health, water supply and sanitation—are considered for providing
support under the Central Pool with projects in physical infrastructure sector receiving priority.
Only project specific assistance is released from the NLCPR and no diversion is permissible.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
The Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) became operational in April,
1998. The pool has come into existence out of the shortfalls in the stipulated expenditure
norm of 10% by each Central Ministry/Department for the North-Eastern region. The total
amount accrued to this pool during 1998-2002 was Rs.5806.07 crore. Thus, on an average a
little over Rs.1400 crore accrued to NLCPR. Consequent upon the exercise undertaken by
DoNER to ascertain the actual size of the pool, Rs.2853.97 crore were calculated to be
available in it as on 1 April, 2002, after taking into account the debits. However, only
Rs.1318.66 crore have been released to the States during 1998-2002. The release of
Rs.1318.66 crore during 1998-2002 is less than 50% of the cost of the sanctioned projects
worth Rs.2728 crore. (Para 25)
As on date, a total of 548 projects have been sanctioned out of NLCPR with an
approved cost of Rs.3097.24 crore. In sharp contrast to that only Rs.1868.66 crore have
actually been released leaving a committed liability of Rs.1228.58 crore. Against this
requirement, a provision of only Rs.550 crore has been made in BE 2003-04. (Para 25.1)
The above figures clearly indicate that the amount being released out of this central
pool of resources is far less than the accruals to it. There are two aspects of the mechanism
evolved to ensure adequate flow of funds to the process of socio-economic development in
the North-Eastern region. One, Central Ministries/Departments (except for a few exempted)
are required to earmark 10% of their gross budgetary support exclusively for North-Eastern
region. However, statistics prove that Central Ministries/Departments have only been, able
to spend in the range of 6 to 7% out of the earmarked 10% of their gross budgetary
support. (Para 25.2)
The second aspect flows from the first one. The inability of the Central Ministries/
Departments to spend the whole of the 10%, paved the way for creation of NLCPR which
is, as stated elsewhere, constituted of the shortfalls in the stipulated expenditure norm of
10%. As stated in the preceding paragraphs, the release of funds out of this pool is less
than 50% of its actual size. (Para 25.2.1)
After having had a look at the two aspects of the mechanism evolved to ensure flow
of funds, it becomes amply clear that neither 10% norm nor NLCPR has been able to
maintain a steady flow of funds. Although, on an average Rs.1400 crore accrue to this pool
every year, the annual release out of it has hovered around Rs.300 crore or so. This proves
that there is a clear mismatch between the accruals and the release of funds. As against
a projected requirement of Rs.1050 crore for 2003-04, the Planning Commission has
approved only Rs.550 crore. The amount sanctioned by Planning Commission is on the lower
side keeping in view the fact that Sikkim has also become part of the North-Eastern region.
In this way, the purpose behind setting up of NLCPR is getting defeated as adequate funds
are not flowing out of it. (Para 25.3)
25.4 In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Government should not
only release the backlog amount of Rs.1228.58 crore out of NLCPR to enable the DoNER
13

14
to maintain the momentum of developmental activities in the North-Eastern region but it
should also ensure pro rata release of funds out of total accruals to NLCPR henceforth.
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
During Ninth Five Y ear Plan, an outlay of Rs. 2114 crore was made for NEC. Out of
that Rs.1970.90 crore were allocated to it and Rs.1937.71 crore were actually spent by
it. The annual allocation during the plan period progressively grew from Rs.324 crore in
1997-98 to Rs. 450 crore in the terminal year i.e. 2001-02. Similarly, during the Tenth Plan,
the Planning Commission has made an outlay of Rs.3500 crore for NEC. Out of this
plan outlay, Rs.450 crore were allocated for 2002-03 which has now been enhanced to
Rs.500 crore.
Thus, the pattern of allocations to NEC followed during the Ninth Plan is being
adhered to in the Tenth Plan also. In other words, the flow of funds to NEC continues to
be progressive in nature starting with lower allocation in the first year and then gradually
going up with the progression of the Plan. In contrast to NEC’s projection of Rs. 800 crore
for 2003-04, only Rs. 500 crore have been provided to it and that too when Sikkim has
recently joined as the eighth member of the Council.
Here, the Committee would like to emphasise the point that annual allocations out
of plan outlay should be on the higher side in the initial years of the plan period so that
the projected activities get underway with a head start. The Committee is of the view that
the maximum momentum should be provided in the beginning of the Plan so that its steady
progression is maintained in later years also. Besides, as a Plan progresses, the value of the
allocations in real terms declines with the passage of time. Therefore, by providing a
sizeable chunk of the outlay in the first two years of the Plan, an optimum use of the funds
can be made. In this background, the Committee is of the view that the Government should
enhance NEC’s allocation as per actual requirements projected by it.
In addition, the Government may also consider to place the unutilised funds of the
NLCPR at the disposal of the North-Eastern Council. (Para 26, 26.1, 26.2 and 26.3)
The North-Eastern Council has recently been remodelled as a regional planning body
with its emphasis on projects and schemes involving two or more States. Over the years,
NEC has, primarily, been playing the role of a central funding agency. As a result, it has
not been able to focus its attention on a balanced regional growth. In the absence of a
comprehensive planning for the region aimed at all-round development, the North-Eastern
region continues to lag behind. The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that the
North-Eastern Council should play a proactive role in the development of the North-Eastern
region while focusing its attention on regional planning. (Para 27)
VRS PACKAGE FOR SIKKIM MINING CORPORATION
28. Sikkim Mining Corporation has been incurring losses ever since it came into
existence. Efforts to revive it by way of providing budgetary grants and loans have proved
futile. As a result of that the burden of losses, interests, salaries, etc. continues to mount.
With a view to bring about a turnaround in the ailing PSU, a restructuring plan was
submitted by DoNER to the Planning Commission which has since been rejected by it. After
the rejection of restructuring plan, there is another proposal which seeks to rationalise the
manpower of the corporation by offering ‘Voluntary Retirement Scheme’ package which
entails an expenditure of Rs.2.5 crore. The implementation of this VRS package is expected
to reduce the burden of salaries to the employees to a great extent which, in turn, will help

15
in putting the loss making PSU back on track. Therefore, the Committee recommends that
the VRS package for the employees of Sikkim Mining Corporation should be put through
at the earliest. (Para 28)
IMPROVEMENT IN ROAD INFRASTRUCTURE
Roads are an important engine of growth. For a region as remote as the North-East,
the development of a good network of roads is a sine qua non for an all-round socio-
economic development. There is an urgent need to take necessary steps to bring about
qualitative and visible improvement in the condition of roads. For, poor condition of roads
will prove to be a big hurdle in attracting private investment in various sectors. Therefore,
keeping in view the crucial importance of a good road network, the Committee recommends
that a comprehensive action plan should be formulated by the Government to improve,
expand and maintain a durable and reliable road network in the North-Eastern region.
(Para 29)
TECHNOLOGY MISSIONS
30. North-Eastern region is full of natural resources such as medicinal plants, bamboo,
horticulture, floriculture, agricultural products such as ginger and potato, etc. These natural
products have a potential to catapult the region to the position of being a major base for
agri-business and agri-exports. Another bountiful natural resource is water which can be
harnessed in a big way to generate hydel-electricity. The hydel-electricity potential of the
region is 32000 MW which, if realised optimally, can transform the region as the
powerhouse of the country. Similarly, oil and natural gas is also a major potential area
which could prove to be a big help in import substitution.
30.1. Undoubtedly, the North-Eastern region is a resource-rich area. But the abundant
resources of the region have remained untapped. Consequently, it has lagged behind in the
national process of development. Today, the region is beset with multiple problems such as
unemployment, economic backwardness, low industrial development, poor social and
economic infrastructure etc. In order to overcome these problems, concerted, well-
coordinated, focused and persistent efforts are needed.
30.2 The Committee, therefore, is of the considered opinion that the Government should
launch ‘Technology Missions’ with a view to harness the immense potential of various areas
within a fixed time-frame. (Para 30, 30.1 and 30.2)
PROMOTION OF TOURISM
31. North-Eastern States are not rich just in natural resources but they are also endowed
with pristine natural beauty. This virgin beauty has, however, remained beyond the reach
of people from other parts of the country as well as foreigners due to a variety of reasons
such as poor tourist infrastructure, lack of adequate rail and air services, less exposure to
the outside world, spread of insurgency-related violence in various parts, etc. All these and
many other factors have contributed to the non-realisation of the potential of the tourism
sector.
31.1 As the times are changing and the region is now getting more and more exposed
coupled with a strong urge among the people to attain economic prosperity and self-
sufficiency, the time is opportune to showcase the region as a major tourist destination.
Therefore, the Committee is of the view that a comprehensive plan should be prepared and
implemented to give the much-needed boost to the tourism industry in the North-Eastern
region. The Committee hopes that such a step will prove to be a major turning point in the
economic development of the region. (Para 31 and 31.1)

Delimitation Commission
4. Budget Estimates of Election Commission for the year 2003-2004 includes the budgetary
allocation of Delimitation Commission. The parameters for the working of the Delimitation
Commission are contained in the Delimitation Act, 2002 and have also been detailed in the guidelines
framed by the Commission. Pursuant to the enactment of the Constitution (Eighty-fourth
Amendment) Act, 2001, the Delimitation Act, 2002 was enacted. The Delimitation Commission is
a three member body constituted on 12.7.2002, under the provisions of the Delimitation Act, 2002
# Grants of Supreme Court is charged.
∉  Approximately.

3
with Shri Justice Kuldip Singh, a retired Judge of the Supreme Court, as its Chairperson and
Shri B.B. Tandon, one of the Election Commissioners and the third Member of the Commission is
the Election Commissioner of the concerned State that is being delimited. The main task of the
Commission is to readjust the division of territorial constituencies of the seats in the House of the
People allocated to each State and the readjustment of the division of territorial constituencies of
the total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of each State. The rationalisation of the
constituencies shall be on the basis of the 1991 census figures. The Commission will also refix
the seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes on the basis of that census.
The Commission has started functioning with the secretarial assistance from the Election
Commission of India and is expected to complete its work within two years.
4.1 When asked about the guidelines for the Associate Members of the Commission, the
Government in its written reply stated that under the provisions of the Delimitation Act, 2002, the
Commission is required to delimit the Assembly and Parliamentary Constituencies in respect of all
States (excepting Jammu and Kashmir) and the UT of Pondicherry and NCT of Delhi. As per
guidelines the Commission prepares Paper-1 and Paper-2 in respect of each State relating to
distribution of total assembly seats among various districts and entitlement of the seats to be
reserved for Scheduled Castes to various districts respectively in each State. These papers are yet
to be prepared in respect of Assam, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Manipur, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh and West
Bengal where the data of 1991 census prepared and submitted by the Chief Electoral Officers is
being checked for correctness in the Commission.
4.2 The Working Papers (which includes Paper-l and Paper-2) containing detailed proposals
have already been prepared and discussed with the Associate Members from the States of Goa,
Mizoram, Rajasthan and Sikkim. They have been asked to send their dissenting notes and after
receiving their dissenting notes, if any, draft proposals will be published in the State and Central
Gazettes inviting objections and suggestions from the public.
4.3 In respect of the States of Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh,
Haryana, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh and NCT of Delhi, Papers-l and 2 have been sent to the
Associate members who are requested to attend meetings fixed during the period of 1st April to
17th April, 2003. The Members have been requested to give their proposals in writing at the
respective meetings so as to enable the Commission to prepare Working Papers with full proposals
on the basis of the suggestions made by them.
4.4 Out of the eleven remaining States, fresh nomination of 5 MLAs each as Associate Members
from the States of Himachal Pradesh, Tripura, Nagaland and Meghalaya after the formation of new
Legislative Assemblies in February, 2003 are awaited. As soon as the Associate Members are
nominated by the Hon’ble Speakers of the respective Legislative Assemblies, Paper-l and 2 relating
to these States will be sent to the Associate members calling them for meetings.
4.5 For the remaining seven States of Bihar , Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Pondicherry, Tamil
Nadu and Uttaranchal, Papers-l and 2 are ready, and the dates for first meetings will be fixed in
due course.
4.6 When asked about adoption of 1971 procedure instead of framing new procedure, the
Department in its written reply stated that in substance the procedure followed by the Commission
is by and large the same as followed by the 1971 Commission. The Minister of Law and Justice
sent a letter to the Commission on 17 March, 2003 conveying general feeling at the all political
parties’ meeting held on March 13, 2003 regarding consultation with Associate Members in the
process of formulation of draft delimitation proposals. In deference to the general feeling expressed
at the said meeting, the Commission have decided to adopt the revised Guidelines for the
delimitation of constituencies under the Delimitation Act, 2002.

to the views of the Associate Members while carrying out the delimitation exercise and has
endeavoured to do this. However, since it has been brought to the notice of the Delimitation
Commission that there is some dissatisfaction amongst Associate Members on the methodology that
has been adopted by the Commission while carrying out its functions, the Delimitation Commission

AFFAIRS
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)
7.0 The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs in his deposition before the Committee stated
that the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal which decides appeals against the orders of the
Departmental authorities in respect of all direct taxes, has a pendency of 1,82,625 cases at the end
of February, 2003. Number of measures have been adopted to reduce pendency of cases such as
clubbing of cases having similar issues, identification of small cases for quick disposal,
identification of cases involving issues already covered by the decisions of the Supreme Court,
raising the limit from Rs.l lakh to Rs.5 lakh for appeals to be heard by a single Member, formation
of mobile Benches etc. As a result of these measures the increase in pendency has been arrested
and it is going down. Most of the Benches of ITAT are housed in private accommodation taken
on rent. There is also a problem of providing suitable residential accommodation to Members of
ITAT. On these aspects a public interest litigation is pending in the Supreme Court and the Supreme
Court has been issuing directions from time to time regarding providing office accommodation as
well as accommodation for residential purposes for the Members of ITAT. The Department has
been trying to meet the directions of the Supreme Court within the available financial resources and
there is a genuine need to construct office accommodation for various Benches of ITAT as also
to provide residential accommodation to Members of ITAT. The Department sought the support of
the this Committee for the construction of infrastructure for the Tribunal so as to ensure smooth
and efficient discharge of its functions.
7.1 The Committee recommends that the Government should explore the possibility of
including the financial proposals for the requirement of accommodation for official as well as
residential purposes for the ITAT under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the Development
of Infrastructural Facilities for the Judiciary through hundred per cent central funding.
